utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A very good morning to everybody. May I ask Madam Registrar, please, to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-14/2-A, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may we have the appearances, please. For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for the Prosecution is Norman Farrell, Ms. Helen Brady, Ms. Michelle Jarvis, Ms. Marie-Ursula Kind; and also Mr. Geoffrey Nice, the senior trial attorney from trial, will be sitting in court with the appeals team. Our case manager is Ms. Lourdes Galicia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farrell. May I ask for the Defence of Mr. Kordic. Mr. Naumovski, Mr. Sayers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Stephen Sayers, I will be appearing with my colleague Mr. Turner Smith, and my Croatian colleague Mr. Mitko Naumovski. Our case manager is Mr. Zayne Tweed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Defence for Mr. Cerkez. Mr. Kovacic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I am appearing together with my colleague Mr. Goran Mikulicic as Defence counsel for Mr. Cerkez. My name is Bozidar Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask both Mr. Kordic and Mr. Cerkez, first you feel fit today for hearing the case, following the proceedings, in particular in a language you understand? THE APPELLANT KORDIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. Thank you for inquiring. Yes, I can understand and follow the proceedings without problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Please. THE APPELLANT CERKEZ: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I feel very well, and I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated as well. Before starting, let me turn to a short introduction. In October 1997, Mr. Dario Kordic and Mr. Mario Cerkez voluntarily surrendered to this Tribunal. The trial proceedings commenced in April 1999 and ended in December 2000. On 26 February 2001, Trial Chamber III rendered a judgement, sentencing Dario Kordic to 25 years of imprisonment, and Mario Cerkez to 15 years of imprisonment. They were both found guilty for the majority of the 44 counts of the amended indictment of the 30th of September, 1998, inter alia, crimes against humanity, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, and violations of the laws or customs of war, including persecutions, murder, unlawful attacks on civilian persons and property, inhumane treatment, and the destruction or wilful damage to institutions dedicated to religion or education. The Trial Chamber found that these crimes were committed during an international armed conflict between Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats in 1992 and 1993 in Central Bosnia, in particular in Lasva Valley. The population of this area in 1991 was nearly 470.000 citizens, of whom about 48 per cent were Muslims, 32 per cent Croats, and 10 per cent Serbs. According to the Trial Chamber, in late 1991, the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a branch of the Croatian Democratic Union of the Republic of Croatia, set up Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, a separate Croat community within Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the intention that it should accede to the Republic of Croatia. Thereafter, the Croatian Defence Council, HVO, was established as the executive and Defence authority of the Bosnian Croat community in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Dario Kordic, according to the Appeals Chamber, was a political leader in the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, president of the Croatian Democratic Union in Busovaca, and finally, vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Mario Cerkez was one of the founders of the HVO in Vitez and finally commander of the Viteska Brigade. The Trial Chamber held that a campaign of persecutions aimed at the Bosnian Muslims took place in Central Bosnia, including the attacks on towns and villages with concomitant destruction and plunder, killing, injuring and detaining of Bosnian Muslims. According to the Trial Chamber, the campaign to ethnically cleanse Lasva Valley of Muslims was led by the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina and conducted through instruments of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO and orchestrated from Zagreb. The Trial Chamber found that Dario Kordic was a political leader and played a principal role by planning, preparing, and ordering those acts of the campaign which fell in his sphere of authority. Mario Cerkez participated in the execution of the plan by commanding the Viteska Brigade during the attacks on Vitez, Stari Vitez, and Donja Veceriska. Both Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez were held individually responsible pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute. In addition, Mario Cerkez was also found guilty pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute based on his superior responsibility and failure to prevent these crimes committed during the attacks and to punish those who were responsible for them. The Trial Chamber held that the well-organised and planned HVO attacks in Lasva Valley culminated in the massacre in the village of Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, where more than 100 Bosnian Muslims were murdered, including 32 women and 11 children. The Trial Chamber was convinced that Dario Kordic was present at meetings where the attack on Ahmici was authorised and that he was associated with an order to kill all military-aged men, expel the civilians, and set fire to houses in Ahmici. As regards Mario Cerkez, however, the Trial Chamber was not satisfied that he bore any responsibility for the attack on Ahmici. The Trial Chamber found beyond reasonable doubt that during the HVO offences, many hundreds of Bosnian Muslim civilians were arbitrarily and unlawfully detained in makeshift camps as part of a common plan and held under inhumane conditions. The Trial Chamber held that Dario Kordic was responsible for the unlawful imprisonment of detainees in the area for which he had authority. Mario Cerkez, as commander of the Viteska Brigade, was held responsible for unlawful imprisonment and inhuman treatment committed in the detention facilities in Vitez. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber found that the common plan comprised a pattern of unjustified destruction, plunder in the locations attacked by the HVO at mosques, and other religious and educational institutions were deliberately targeted. It held that Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez were involved in these offences in those places where they had been finally found responsible for attacks. This judgement was appealed by all parties for different, sometimes overlapping, reasons. Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez base their respective fundamental appeals on numerous alleged errors of both fact and law. In their opinion, also the sentences are not justified. The Prosecutor has appealed the acquittal of Mario Cerkez in relation to the crimes committed during the attack on Ahmici. She has also appealed the sentences meted out by the Trial Chamber against Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez. During the pre-appeal proceedings, various grounds of appeal were withdrawn, not the least due to the further developed jurisprudence in the Tribunal since February 2001. In relation to some of the locations mentioned in the charges, the Prosecution has conceded that the trial judgement does not contain factual findings. In this context, I would like to refer particularly to pages 163 to 165 of the transcript of the pre-appeal conference held the 6th of May, 2004. I have to recall once again that an appeals hearing is not the place to re-argue the case. As regards the scope of an appeal, all parties have received the relevant parts of the Kunarac appeal judgement. In this context, I want to repeat my current request to all parties: When referring to a document or transcript, please mention the number or page number in concreto already in the beginning of the relevant submissions so that we can have the same document before us. Please also indicate when you have concluded your argument on a concrete point, giving, hereby, the Judges a chance to put questions to you, if necessary, without interrupting your line of thoughts. The Appeals Chamber will focus today on the appeal lodged by Dario Kordic, tomorrow primarily on Mario Cerkez's appeal, and finally, on Wednesday, on the appeal of the Prosecutor. Instead of paraphrasing in more detail the various grounds of appeal raised by the parties, I should like to give, without further ado, the floor to the Defence of Dario Kordic. Mr. Sayers, I understand that Mr. Kordic's Defence has split up the submissions amongst counsel. Who wants to take the floor first? Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Let me just say by way of introduction that the principal appellate briefs in this case were filed three years ago. In all candour, they look a little fossilised in light of the jurisprudence that has been developed by the Appeals Chamber in the intervening three years. They have a certain antique look to them. For that reason, we have prepared a very visual presentation today focused specifically on the points of appeal which we consider to be the most important. Slides that will come up on the screen will have detailed references to the exhibit numbers, page numbers of the transcript, and most pertinently, to paragraph numbers of intervening Appeals Chamber judgements and Trial Chamber judgements decided over the last three years. As the Appeals Chamber is well aware, there has been significant development in the jurisprudence relating to the level of specificity required in pleadings. The concept of joint criminal enterprise has virtually been developed since 2001, when I do not believe there had ever been references by that name to that concept of liability. I am sure I do not need to remind the Appeals Chamber of the enormous girth of this case. According to one representative of the Tribunal, this was the longest war crimes trial ever tried, at least before the Milosevic case, which is just about half over, as I understand it. There were over 241 witnesses who testified, because many testified by transcripts from other cases. There were 4.665 exhibits in this case, many of which popped up, as the Appeals Chamber knows, in the middle of trial, towards the end of trial, and right at the end of the trial. Indeed, the appeals process has been protracted for three years largely because of -- it's difficult to find an appropriate adjective, but let's just say a protracted period of continual disclosures under a rule which features very centrally in this case, Rule 68. In fact, last Thursday we received two more disclosures, one relating to ABiH plans to attack the Croats in the Lasva Valley, the other one relating to detentions and a report from Zlatko Aleksovski to his commander, Colonel Blaskic, on the conditions in the detention facilities. That wasn't the last disclosure. We received another one on Friday, the 14th of May. This was a detailed synopsis of proceedings in the district military courts prepared by the district military prosecutor of the HVO, Zeljko Percinlic. The organisation of the argument I have set out on the slide that's before the trial. I will take care of the fair trial issues. Dario Kordic contends that he did not receive equality of arms. There were numerous Rule 68 violations. Indeed, violations more serious than in any case tried before this Tribunal, and in fact more serious than in any national jurisdiction of which I am aware. These violations go to the root of a fair trial in this Tribunal. I will then proceed to look at the unacceptably vague indictment in this case, an indictment which I must say presented the apparently irresistible opportunity to the Prosecution to mount a moving target case against Mr. Kordic. We had no idea from month-to-month what theory of liability was being pursued against Mr. Kordic, and it changed, and it changed radically right at the end of the case from a national case over 31 municipalities over a huge period of time, to one single meeting on one afternoon on one day. Nowhere alleged in the amended indictment. I will then deal with the central witness in this case, Witness AT, who talked about that meeting. And the two paragraphs which are absolutely central to the Trial Chamber's findings are paragraphs 630 and 631 of the trial judgement. We'll be paying considerable attention to those. In addition, we are aware of no case before this Tribunal, none whatsoever, where a conviction has been based upon purely uncorroborated hearsay from a single witness, especially a witness such as this, a convicted murderer, a self-confessed liar, and a man who attempted to perpetrate a fraud on this Tribunal, on his own Trial Chamber, on the Appeals Chamber and, we would argue, on the Kordic Trial Chamber too. I will then proceed to authentication and Exhibit Z610.1 in particular, the book of observations of an unidentified duty officer prepared at a time unknown by persons unknown and for which there was no authentication. The three witnesses who addressed it testified variously, one, that there were anomalies that could not being explained; two, that components of this document had been faked and fabricated; and three, that the document did not appear to be a military document in the normal format. I will then proceed, if I have time, to deal with the Rule 98 bis issues and also armed conflict and international armed conflict. The Appeals Chamber asked us to address count-by-count the findings of the Trial Chamber. The Appeals Chamber cannot be unaware that that's almost impossible to do because each doubt has numerous individual locations. So the way we've tried to do it is to break down the elements of the crime and proceed meticulously, location by location, to analyse whether the elements of the crime as to each location have been made out. Mr. Smith will also address the law of persecution which, as the Trial Chamber noted, was the broadest count in this indictment. I would say to call it the broadest count in this indictment would be an understatement of great dimensions. Mr. Naumovski will then proceed to examine the same sorts of things with respect to village-specific locations. I've actually got the order reversed on this slide here; he's going to deal with the Kiseljak area first. Again, convictions there based apparently upon the uncorroborated testimony of a single witness, Witness Y, and establishing what? That Mr. Kordic was present at a particular place at a particular time. Not that he was doing anything, because the witness didn't hear Mr. Kordic say anything, didn't see him do anything; mere presence. And in light of the jurisprudence from this Tribunal within the last month in the Krstic case, the Potocari incidents specifically addressed in paragraph 98 and 149 and 248 of that opinion, that's a finding which has particular pertinence. And I will conclude with the sentencing appeal. Turning first to the general standards of appellate review. I had intended to spend some time on that, but I'm happy to say that our efforts in that regard were fruitfully truncated. The Kunarac appeals judgement provides the governing standards of review, so I won't go into those particularly. We acknowledge that as to errors of law, it's our burden to prove that the error of law affected the outcome. We will look at substantive errors of law and procedural errors that were committed by the Trial Chamber. As to errors of fact, again we concede not every error of fact results in an acquittal or a reversal. We have to show that the error of fact has resulted in a miscarriage of justice. What is that? A miscarriage of justice occurs when there has been a grossly unfair outcome such as, for example, when a defendant is convicted of offences in the absence of factual findings, which we know has occurred here, despite a lack of evidence on essential elements of the crime, which we will go into in detail. The key concept in any case like this is a very simple concept in essence: It's linkage. In the Delalic appeals judgement, the Appeals Chamber emphasised that it is the Prosecution's burden to prove the link of control and great care must be taken lest an injustice be done in holding someone accountable where the link of control is absent or too remote. Nor is this any mystery in this case, because in the closing argument held on the 14th of December, 2000, this precise point was made to the Prosecution by the Presiding Judge and conceded by the Prosecution. That is the issue in this case, as the Presiding Judge said, the link of control, linkage with crimes and the establishment of the necessary mens rea for the imposition of criminal culpability for those crimes. As the Prosecution itself has acknowledged in its brief, linkage is what counts in this case, and Kordic's position is that no linkage was established. I might just say that the Galic trial judgement issued in December of last year made the point that there are only two cases which have examined the concept of an attack on civilians; Blaskic and Kordic. Now, it's true that Galic probably is the third case, but there is no jurisprudence from this Chamber on the law relating to attacks on civilians, although there is some evidence that the Kunarac -- from the Kunarac Appeals Chamber that emphasises that in order to establish an attack on civilians, the civilian population must be the primary, not merely an incidental, target of the attack. Just a word on burden of proof. I'm sure I don't need to spend a lot of time on this. It's pretty obvious. The Prosecution bears the burden of proof at all times, arguably even on appeal, of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, but more importantly, as to each element of each offence. Failure to prove it with respect to any element of an offence results in an acquittal. Furthermore, it bears emphasis that even the gravest of suspicion, as was the case in the Simic contempt judgement where Mr. Avramovic was found not guilty of contempt of this Tribunal, but even the gravest suspicion cannot prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Circumstantial evidence, the centre of the conviction against Mr. Kordic, paragraph 13 of the judgement in this case described variously by the Prosecution as subtle, difficult, and complex. A great deal of evidence which goes one way goes the other, says the Prosecution in the opening statement. How important, then, is it to make sure that the Prosecution discharges in a subtle, difficult, and complex case its fundamental duty of disclosing in a timely fashion exculpatory evidence, or to use the apt phraseology of the Rule, as soon as practicable. Because it's the Prosecution that has to prove the case, not the other way around, as the Presiding Judge reminded the Prosecution at TR28306. In fact, during the closing argument the Presiding Judge made the point to the Prosecution that much of your case hangs on inferences, and that's exactly where we are. The law of inferences we've summarised on this slide. For an inference to be reached it must be the only inference that can reasonably be reached on the evidence. If there's another conclusion available on that evidence, then it is the duty of the Trial Chamber to acquit. The Trial Chamber, of course, cannot draw the inference least favourable to the accused. It is Mr. Kordic's position that that happened time and again in this case, and we would submit that it is apparent from looking at the judgement. Thirdly, and equally significantly, the Vasiljevic Appeals judgement issued this year, just two months ago, made the point with respect to mens rea that where mens rea is based upon inferences, special attention must be paid to the acts of the accused because if the acts of the accused are ambiguous, then he cannot be convicted. Here it's difficult to say what the basis of the conviction was because no acts of Mr. Kordic were really specified in the central paragraphs, paragraph 630 and 631, of the judgement. All we know is, from Witness AT, that Mr. Kordic was supposedly present at a particular place at a particular time. We have no idea what was said. In fact, we have no idea who said what because no one was present at the central meeting. There's no proof of that whatsoever and, therefore, nothing which would allow an inference one way or the other as to what Mr. Kordic would have said if he had been there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down a little. Could the counsel be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please slow down a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The law of inferences was canvassed on the 14th of December, 2000, and concessions were made by the Prosecution that the law is as I have just outlined it. And I have highlighted the transcript reference on this slide 28303 to 304. Turning to our first specific ground of appeal, ground of appeal 1-D, we were asked in the pre-appeal stage to address timely access. Mr. Kordic takes the position that even if equality of arms means only equal access to procedural relief, if that's all it means in this Tribunal, and that is apparently what the law is, if that's the narrow definition of what equality of arms does mean, then Mr. Kordic was denied it. He made a motion for access to closed-session materials in the related Lasva Valley cases before trial; denied. During trial twice; denied. Oh, and why? Because the Prosecution had represented to the Trial Chamber not once but twice that all exculpatory evidence had been produced, and it had not been, as the Appeals Chamber is well aware. The exculpatory evidence of General Blaskic was that Mr. Kordic was nowhere to be seen in the HVO chain of command. Nowhere. He was a civilian. General Blaskic was not subordinated to Mr. Kordic in any sense whatsoever. None of that was produced to Mr. Kordic while, simultaneously, the Prosecution was seeking the imposition of a life sentence against Mr. Kordic under a theory of command responsibility pursuant to Article 7(3) of this Tribunal's Statute. Now, equality of arms is a very important concept. What's it designed to do? It is designed to make sure that parties are free to present their case under conditions that do not put them at a disadvantage vis-a-vis the other party. In the Hadzihasanovic case, the Trial Chamber emphasised that the Defence is always entitled to seek material facts from any source to assist it in its case, which is what Mr. Kordic did, but as I've said, those efforts were -- those efforts were unsuccessful. Now, how is this depicted by the Prosecution? Well, we know this is depicted as a genuinely troubling episode according to the consolidated respondent's brief paragraph 2.22. There was nothing episodic about this non-disclosure or belated disclosure. It continued throughout the case, and before the case, actually. Take a look, for example, at Witness AT. When did this witness testify? One week before the close of all of the evidence. Exhibit Z610.1. When did this exhibit come into evidence? December 1, 2000, one week before the close of all of the evidence. Under Article 21(4)(a) and (b), fair trial guarantees demand that an accused have fair notice of the charges against him so that he has adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence. Associated issues are Rule 68, the right to timely access to exculpatory material at a time when the accused still enjoys the presumption of innocence, when the burden of proof is affirmatively upon the Prosecution to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt as to each element of each offence, and when the accused still enjoys the benefit of all inferences in his favour. Before trial, an order was entered compelling the Prosecution to turn over exculpatory material and witness statements. And why? Well, we know: Proper protection of the rights of the accused is overriding. And that order was particularly appropriate because, as we've stated on the slide before this Appeals Chamber, the Prosecution had plenty of time to get it right. Five years of investigations before this trial began, as Mr. Goldstone told Judge McDonald in 1995, full support of the Muslim authorities of the Federation, as the representative of the Muslim authorities of the Federation assured the Trial Chamber again in 1995. Four entire trials: Furundzija, Aleksovski, Kupreskic, Blaskic. Hundreds of witnesses, thousands of exhibits. There is no excuse for the frenzy that occurred at the first few months of this case, with continual disclosures of literally tens of thousands of pages of documents upon Kordic. When he should be preparing to get the trial under way, he was still discovering what the Prosecution's case assertedly was. Why is timely disclosure important? The order entered on Rules 68 and 66 on 26 February 1999 made this point, and it made it cogently, in our view. It permits the Defence to get a clear and cohesive view of the Prosecution's strategy and to make appropriate preparations. We never had that opportunity. Despite having plenty I have time to get it right, as we said, the Prosecution moved for extensions of time right before the trial, and those motions were granted. We received, I believe, some 361 witness statements, plus associated documentation, not simply a month before trial, but a month into the trial. The Kupreskic appeals judgement made appropriate observations with respect to the fairness of such a procedure. I believe the witness statements regarding Witness H, the central witness in that case, indeed the linchpin of the evidence in that case, were delivered to the Defence one month before the trial began. When were the statements of Witness AT delivered to Mr. Kordic? September and early October 2000, one and a half years after the trial had started. The moving target presented to us raises questions of fairness. As the appeals -- as the Presiding Judge stated, the Trial Chamber ought to know the case it has to decide by the end of the Prosecution case, a relatively elementary point, it might be thought. Well, if it was reasonable for the Trial Chamber to know the case it had to decide before this -- before the Prosecution rested its case, surely it was not unreasonable for the Defence to know the case it had to meet before the end of the Prosecution's case. And for our other arguments on this point, we rely upon our brief. Let me turn now to Rule 68. There are three versions of Rule 68 that have applied throughout the protracted history of this case. The differences in the Rule make no difference in this case, because the overriding obligation is still the same. The Prosecution must disclose, as soon as practicable, exculpatory evidence. This is not a difficult rule to understand. As I stated in my opening comments, the non-disclosures here are the worst example of non-disclosures in any reported case in this Tribunal, far worse than in Krstic, just a month ago, worse than in any other case in my national jurisdiction of which I am aware, even worse than the egregious non-disclosures involved in the case decided by the United States Supreme Court two months ago, Banks. Now, what are the sources of the obligations of disclosure here? It's not simply Rule 68. There were two separate orders entered by two separate Trial Chambers, this one and the Blaskic Trial Chamber, before the trial began, ordering disclosure of any exculpatory evidence to Kordic from the closed-session materials in the Blaskic case and otherwise. Exculpatory evidence must be disclosed, if it's available, before trial. Here it was available. It should have been produced as soon as practicable. What's the importance of Rule 68? The Tadic appeals judgement made by the point that the right to a fair trial is central to the rule of law. It upholds due process of law. Indeed, the Prosecution has recognised that disclosure obligations must be fulfilled by its office and that that is essential for a fair trial. Ironically, this was in a pleading that was filed two months before the Prosecution's consolidated respondent's brief in this case, contending that it hadn't violated Rule 68 in any way. Furthermore, three years ago, the point was made - and it was reiterated two months ago in the Blaskic Appeals Chamber - that the obligation to disclose is not a secondary one, to be accomplished after everything else has been done. It is as important as the obligation to prosecute. But apparently in this case, that is not the case to the Prosecution. The obligation here, in the Prosecution's view, is a secondary one, and it's only to be complied with after everything else has been done, after a conviction has been obtained, partially, I might add, through the suppression of critical exculpatory evidence, and discharged only after the accused has found out about the non-disclosure as a result of his own motions practice, fortuitously stumbling across references to the concealed material in the Prosecution's other confidential submissions in other cases. The importance of the Prosecution's obligations under Rule 68 can scarcely be overemphasised. The principle of a fair trial cannot be frustrated by the Prosecution's inability to disclose exculpatory evidence. That is an observation made when the Prosecution was saying, "We have so much material, it's very difficult to sift through it all, please allow us a little latitude in disclosing this because of the magnitude of the materials we have to go through." But not in this case. Because as the Appeals Chamber knows from submissions made in this case, this wasn't a mistake. We had originally thought that this non-disclosure was a mistake, that the matter just got lost in the shuffle, as it were, that it was the product of overwork, perhaps inadvertence, perhaps negligence. But it wasn't. It was deliberate. The Prosecution's Blaskic trial team prepared summaries of the extensive testimony of General Blaskic. They gave them to the Prosecution's trial team in this case. They were looked at, scrutinised, analysed, and the decision was made consciously and deliberately to withhold that material from Kordic. Now, the question is: Is this acceptable conduct before this Tribunal? Actually even asking the question, how could it be? Speaking for myself, in my national jurisdiction, in the lowliest court, the general district court of Fairfax County, in a misdemeanour Prosecution, if exculpatory evidence of this magnitude had been withheld, the prosecutor responsible for it would be subject to the severest of disciplinary sanctions and would probably be disbarred. The scope of the disclosure obligations imposed upon the Prosecution are not mysterious. Rule 68 includes all information in any form that falls within the description of Rule 68, according to the 11th of May, 2001, decision in this case. Material that is exculpatory will of course always be material for the preparation of the Defence, as the Delalic Trial Chamber observed. Rule 68 is a rule that must be interpreted broadly, not narrowly. It one of the most onerous responsibilities of the Prosecution. And why? Because guilt by association is not a concept that is acceptable in this Tribunal or indeed in any tribunal. The Prosecution itself recognises this, and as I've said, the Prosecution in this case sought a life sentence under Article 7(3) based upon the proposition that Mr. Kordic was somehow a military commander. This information was absolutely refuted by General Blaskic but that refutation was deliberately suppressed. General Blaskic's testimony was at all times available to the Prosecution. The closed-session testimony was at all times available to the Prosecution. The closed-session testimony was not available to Kordic until it was ultimately produced, and I will go into the chronology of that in just a minute. How did we find out about it? Well, we asked for access to confidential appellate submissions in other cases, and lo and behold, we find two things: One, in Kupreskic, in a confidential basis, the Prosecution says about Witness AT, "Well, he couldn't have been -- could not conceivably have been aware of the nature and content of the political leadership meeting held in the office of Blaskic on the 15th of April." So that's the Prosecution's submission in the Kupreskic case. Witness AT didn't have a clue about what the nature and content of the political leadership meeting on the 15th of April, 1993 was. And secondly, we find out in the Blaskic case, where apparently General Blaskic's new defence on appeal is that Kordic was exercising covert military power unknown to the military commander of the entire Operative Zone, we find that the Prosecution relies upon the general's own testimony that Kordic exercised no military power at all. Blaskic refutes the proposition that Kordic exercised any military control, according to the Prosecution's confidential submissions. Citing closed-session testimony that Kordic personally was not in the chain of command. He did not function within the chain of command between the military police and the battalion. He was associated only with the civilian authorities. Nonetheless, in its sentencing appeal, the Prosecution urges the Appeals Chamber to increase the sentence upon Mr. Kordic because, it is said, the Trial Chamber failed to take proper account of the powers, positions and responsibilities of Mr. Kordic. The Prosecution has taken inconsistent positions in the various appeals. For example, with respect to Novi Travnik, General Blaskic was not convicted for the events that occurred in Novi Travnik in October 1992. Kordic was. Let's consider the non-disclosed testimony of General Blaskic with respect to those events. As I've said, Kordic was not in the chain of command. You can see that on the screen. As to the Novi Travnik fighting, the general stressed that, "I personally was leading the operations and conducting them while I was there. When I state that I am leading military operations, I am saying that I am commanding the military operations. When I was there, Kordic did not lead any military operations." Now, was any of this ever disclosed to Kordic by the Prosecution? No. Indeed, the Prosecution called witness after witness, most notably Lieutenant Colonel Stewart, to try to establish that Kordic did exercise military power in that location. But look at what the military commander of the entire region says; he did not. We did not have that. The statements of the local or regional political representatives were not, according to General Blaskic, "binding on me. Kordic was not within the framework of my command --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Indeed, in response to a pointed question from the Presiding Judge in the Blaskic Appeals Chamber, here's what the general had to say about his position vis-a-vis Kordic: "I was not subordinated to him at all. His statements and views were never binding on me and I never received them as such." Never disclosed. Banks v. Dretke. I won't spend very much time on this, this is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. just a case from a national jurisdiction. We expressly recognise that. What was suppressed there? In that case, the accused had already been convicted of murder. That conviction was not at issue in Banks versus Dretke. What was at issue was the death sentence imposed upon Banks in the sentencing hearing, and it was at that hearing that the Prosecution withheld from Banks the fact that its principal sentencing witness, Robert Farr, was actually a paid informant, an issue that went directly centrally to the credibility of the Prosecution's principal witness. Withheld. And what did the Supreme Court say? "The suppression by the Prosecution of evidence favourable to an accused upon request violates due process where the evidence is material either to guilt or punishment ..." "The Prosecution's deliberate deception of a court and jurors by the presentation of known false evidence is incompatible with rudimentary demands of justice." And I emphasise "rudimentary." "As soon as practicable"; what does that mean? Is it hard to understand? No. It's the raison d'etre behind Rule 68. Two points in this regard need to be made. First, the raison d'etre behind the disclosure rules is to permit the accused to make effective use of exculpatory material. Effective use at trial so that it can be used in cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses. This means disclosure as soon as practicably possible so that the Defence can use this material in cross-examination of witnesses whom the Prosecution intends to call. Again, I emphasise "at trial." I've said that the decision not to disclose here was deliberate. What's the proof of that, the Appeals Chamber may ask. Just take a look at confidential annex 10 to the -- this says 8th of May, it's actually 8th of March, 2004 Prosecution response. The Prosecution knew what the general had said in closed session, knew exactly what he'd said, and it decided to suppress it. Now, here's what the Krstic appeals judgement had to say just a month ago: "The disclosure of exculpatory material is fundamental to the fairness of proceedings before the Tribunal. Considerations of fairness are the overriding factor in any determination of whether the governing Rule has been breached." And you can see for yourselves, paragraphs 180 and 211: "Grand declarations of general principles, underscoring the need to enforce this Rule as a central component of the right to a fair trial." So the question before this Appeals Chamber is a pretty serious question today. Are these just words or do they mean something? Are the legal principles that the Appeals Chamber has articulated very -- in a timely fashion and in a very affirmative way in Krstic, are they to be enforced? Because if they are to be enforced, they must be enforced in this case. It is unacceptable in any system of civilised justice for the Prosecution to -- to suppress evidence and then to tell the Trial Chamber that it actually has not been suppressed. In this case, there were two express representations made. One was on the 20th of July -- sorry, the 20th of January, 1993, and one was on the 3rd of August -- I said 1993. The 20th of January, 2000, I'm sorry, and the 3rd of August, 2000. That's what really makes the violation in this case egregious, we would submit to the Appeals Chamber. We were seeking the admission of access to the closed-session testimony of other witnesses in the related Lasva Valley cases, Blaskic being one of them. On the 20th of January, just two days after Lieutenant Colonel Stewart had finished his testimony about Novi Travnik, the Prosecution said, "Don't grant this motion, we've disclosed everything. My word on that should be good enough, and if it isn't, I should like to know why." That's exactly what the Prosecution told the Trial Chamber and the Trial Chamber agreed. It denied our motion. The same thing happened on the 3rd of August, 2000, after the Witness AO debacle, after it turned out following Witness AO's testimony that critical exculpatory material had been in existence. The Prosecution knew about it. It had been in its files for years. That material was only delivered after the witness had already testified and left The Hague. As a result of that, we asked for a Krnojelac certification that in fact the Prosecution had complied with all of its obligations under Rule 68. The Trial Chamber was told once again: We've done that. We've disclosed everything. If my word on that isn't good enough, I should like to know why. Again, by that time, the decision not to disclose had been made. As a result, our motions for access were denied at trial. That's an unacceptable situation, we would submit to the Appeals Chamber. Let me turn to the defective indictment in this case. A bad, overly broad indictment leads to a confused, jumbled judgement. It allows the Prosecution to mount a moving target case that is very difficult to follow. Comment was made at the last Status Conference that it's a really difficult issue to find your path through this judgement of the 26th of February, 2001. The obligation to draft a precise, detailed indictment is one of the minimum fair trial guarantees any accused enjoys in this Tribunal under Article 21(4)(a). He has a right to be informed promptly, which means before the trial begins, and in detail, in detail, of the nature and cause of the charge against him. And why? So that he may have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence. The indictment is the primary accusatory instrument in this Tribunal, and it must, in detail, state the material facts underpinning the charges against an accused, and that's stated in no uncertain terms three years ago in the Kupreskic appeals judgement. I emphasise once again: Here there were five years of investigation before the trial began, four entire Lasva Valley trials. There was a full opportunity to amend, if fresh evidence actually did emerge at trial, to amend the indictment to provide the level of specificity required by the law. The indictment, nonetheless, was not amended. Kordic's motions to dismiss the amended indictment as unduly vague were denied. What was the nature and the cause of the charges against Kordic? The Appeals Chamber should pay detailed and particular attention to the case against Kordic as stated in this amended indictment. Paragraph 35: A political, military campaign to persecute and terrorise Bosnian Muslims. Where? Throughout the 31 municipalities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and in the municipality of Zenica. What was Kordic's asserted involvement? And we urge the Appeals Chamber to pay particular attention to paragraphs 25 and 26 of the amended indictment. Here's the involvement of Kordic, in the Prosecution's view, before trial: He had various high-ranking positions. He was a definite and integral and important figure in the whole campaign. He had power, authority, and responsibility to direct, control, and shape its policies and their execution; to prevent, limit, or punish crimes, violations or abuses which occurred or were carried out in this putative campaign. That's the case against Kordic. What case did we have to meet? We know, because the Trial Chamber encapsulated it perfectly in its 6 April 2000 decision. "The Prosecution case relates to the participation of the accused, Dario Kordic, in the highest levels of government, and the Defence should prepare its case accordingly." And that's precisely what we did, Your Honours. That's exactly what we did. We called national politicians, to former Prime Ministers, chiefs of the Main Staff of the HVO, numerous staff officers of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, including General Blaskic's second in command, Major General Filipovic; his Chief of Staff, Brigadier Nakic; and numerous other officers. We called various brigade commanders, not only from the Central Bosnia Operative Zone but from other operative zones. Now, given the case that was made out against Mr. Kordic, what did the judgement conclude? He was not a commander. He was not a superior. He had no position in the HVO chain of command. He had no power to order HVO military units. He had no power to prevent crimes. He lacked effective control over HVO military forces. He had no power to punish. He was not in the highest echelons of government. He was not an architect of the campaign of persecution. He was not the prime mover in it. He was a civilian. He was a regional political leader, but not the only one. So what was he convicted of? Well, it wasn't based upon participation at the highest levels of government. It wasn't based upon the fact or the legal finding that he had the power, authority or responsibility to direct, control, or shape the HVO or HZ HB policies, or the execution of those policies, as charged. Instead, he was convicted of offences and participation in events that were not charged anywhere in the amended indictment. You can search high and low, and you won't see a reference to the meeting of the 15th of April, 1993, which is the linchpin of the conviction, paragraphs 630 and 631. These events are not charged anywhere in the amended indictment let alone in detail as required. Kordic repeatedly objected to the moving target case that the Prosecution was mounting against him at trial. 20th of July; 3rd of August; 25th of September; 12th of October, 2000. We've summarised some of those on this. This is not an argument that was not -- that was crafted specifically for the appeal. This was an objection that was made contemporaneously at trial and on numerous occasions. In fact, the best depiction of what this case was, was from one of the members of the Trial Chamber who described this as a case of juridical impressionism, a very eloquent and accurate visual image, as the Judge was making the point to the Prosecution that the case cannot be constructed as we go along, but it was. That's exactly what it was. Couple of the -- a couple of examples. The Convoy of Joy. There are ten paragraphs of the judgement devoted to this particular incident in June of 1993, months after the principal events that are at issue in the judgement. No mention of it anywhere in the amended indictment, but the best example is the murder case that was mounted, the case within a case, against Mr. Kordic, the alleged murder of Mirsad Delija on the 25th of January, 1993. According to the judgement, the Prosecution case was that Kordic was somehow implicated in this murder but found that his alleged involvement had not been made out. Alleged where? Not in the amended indictment. The law on this area is relatively simple. It's clear and it should be. It comes from the Kupreskic appeals judgement which found that there was a defective indictment in that case. And why? For the same reasons as in this case. There was an additional detail in Kupreskic which is particularly pertinent to this case. The Appeals Chamber commented that it might have some reluctance to acquit an accused who had been convicted simply because of a defective indictment, but it was fortified in its conclusion that that should, nonetheless, be the result in the case because the linchpin of the conviction in that case was the testimony of a single witness, uncorroborated, Witness H, just like in this case. However, Witness H was not a convict. Witness H was a victim, completely candid, a young lady with no criminal record, who did not relate hearsay but related percipient first-hand testimony, visual identification testimony found not to be of sufficient basis by the Appeals Chamber to found a criminal conviction. The parallels between Kupreskic and this case are fairly striking. What are the legal tests? To evaluate an indictment, you must see whether it sets out the material facts, sets out the material facts of the Prosecution case with enough detail to inform a defendant clearly of the charges against him so that he can prepare his defence. Let's go back to the decision on the 98 bis motion from the Trial Chamber. What was the case according to the Trial Chamber? Participation at the highest levels of government. "Prepare your case accordingly, Mr. Kordic." That's what we did. Pleading in detail is a must. If you know the identity of the victim, the time and place of events, you've got to allege it. Here this was the fifth Lasva Valley case. There were no identifications of specific events, no identification of any asserted victims by name, nothing. More importantly, it's essential, as the Rasevic decision just a few days ago emphasised, that it's essential for the accused to know from the indictment just what his proximity to the events at issue is. He's got to know if he's alleged to have committed crimes, what crimes, when, and how. Again it might be thought that that is a relatively elementary proposition, and we submit that it should be elementary. That's exactly what an indictment is supposed to do. It's supposed to tell you, "You committed a crime. Here's when, here's how, and here's who the crime was committed against." And this indictment just doesn't do it. The only exception to that general rule of pleading is, and we fully recognise it, that where the sheer scale of the alleged crimes makes it impracticable to require a higher level of detail, then that level of detail does not have to be given, but here it was hardly impracticable after, as I have said, four full trials. The Prosecution did change its case in mid-trial from a case of participation of the accused at the highest levels of government, over 31 municipalities and Zenica, over three years to two hours in one afternoon on one day in General Blaskic's office. What happened there? Who knows. There wasn't any evidence of that. Who said what? Who knows. The Trial Chamber didn't know. This Appeals Chamber don't know. No one knows. Who saw Kordic actually in the meeting? No one who testified directly. All we've got is hearsay testimony from Witness AT. These were the material facts: That there was a meeting held in the office of General Blaskic on the 15th of April, 1993, at which planning, instigation, and ordering of crimes occurred. Those were the material facts. Where were they alleged? Nowhere in this amended indictment, but they were alleged in a corrected amended indictment filed in the Ljubicic case. Paragraph 23 of that case alleges specifically the meeting on the 15th of April, 1993, presumably now based upon the testimony of Witness AT. Now, the Prosecution is expected to know its case before it goes to trial. This is an elementary principle outlined in the Kupreskic appeals judgement. "If it doesn't plead material facts with enough specificity, doubt must arise as to whether it is fair to the accused for the trial to proceed. It is not acceptable for the Prosecution to omit the material aspects of its main allegations with the aim of moulding the case against the accused in the course of the trial depending on how the evidence unfolds." That's exactly what Kupreskic said, but what happened here? It did -- the Prosecution did precisely what Kupreskic teaches is not permissible. It omitted the material facts with the aim of moulding the case against Kordic depending on how the evidence unfolded, and that's what happened. The allegations in Kupreskic, just as in this case, were broad and imprecise, but actually, if you take a look at Kupreskic, the allegations were even more specific than in this case. Specific dates were mentioned in the amended indictment in that case. Specific allegations about the accused's asserted involvement in paragraph 9 of the indictment in that case. Much more specific than in our amended indictment in this case, Your Honours. The identities of the victims were known in Kupreskic. They were nowhere alleged in this case. In fact, the case against Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic "was dramatically transformed from alleging integral involvement in the preparation to alleging mere presence when the crimes occurred." And that's exactly the kind of transformation that occurred here. The amended indictment in no way particularised what form the alleged participation took, nor does it in Kordic's case. Similarly, and I will defer to Mr. Smith on this, the persecution charges are framed in the amended indictment in the broadest conceivable way. They are umbrella charges, but the Kupreskic -- in fact, the persecution charge was defined in the judgement in paragraph 28 to be the broadest count in the amended indictment. The Prosecution must particularise the material facts relating to persecution. If it does not, then the -- then the indictment is defective. Persecution cannot -- cannot because of its nebulous character be used as a catch-all charge. Pursuant to elementary principles of criminal pleading, it is not sufficient for an indictment to charge a crime in generic terms. An indictment must delve into particulars. And that's what we have here, a defective indictment. Examples of defective indictments, more specific, ironically, than in our case. The Kunarac case, for example, there was a rape of one witness, FWS-50, that was nowhere alleged in the amended indictment. The evidence relating to this was disregarded by the Trial Chamber. The same thing in Naletelic. Evidence regarding the destruction of the mosques in Doljani and Mostar disregarded because they were not alleged anywhere in the indictment, unlike the destruction of a mosque in Sovici. So the Prosecution knew how to plead the destruction but it failed to do so with respect to Doljani and Mostar so those incidents were disregarded. Similarly, we've outlined a portion of the Kupreskic oral argument where the Prosecution said you need to put a list of the individuals you have killed. That's a natural consequence of the crime that you are pleading. Didn't occur in this case. Now, what is a material fact? We are perfectly prepared to be governed by the Prosecution's view of what is a material fact on this issue. A material fact is a fact upon which the verdict is critically dependent. That's according to one of the Prosecution's pleadings in the Blaskic appeal in 2002, and we absolutely agree with it. In the respondent's brief in Blaskic, the Prosecution said that the indictment must set out the particular acts of the accused himself or the particular course of conduct on his part which were alleged to constitute that responsibility. They must be clearly identified. We agree. Take a look at the amended indictment and reach your own judgement upon whether it satisfies those criteria. We would submit it does not. For example, examples of adequate indictments: Hadzihasanovic. The specific dates of massacres by the ABiH and the names of the victims. We've put a reference to an exhibit here, Exhibit Z1190. It's an ironic exhibit in some ways because it is actually an indictment prepared by the ABiH authorities against Mr. Kordic and about 29 other Bosnian Croats. And if you actually take a look at that, prepared as it was under difficult circumstances of wartime, it's pretty specific. It's got the names of witnesses, it's got particular incidents, it's got particular assertions of what Mr. Kordic supposedly did; participated in a planning meeting sometime in mid-April 1993, according to that indictment. It's far more specific than the indictment in this case. Blagojevic: Detailed dates of times and meetings. But most importantly, in Krstic, look at this: Specifically in the indictment it was alleged that there were three meetings, not just on particular days but at particular hours. 2000 hours on 11 July 1995. Three hours later on the same day, 10.00 in the morning on the next day. The Ljubicic corrected amended indictment, we would submit to the Appeals Chamber, is a model of particularity. The material facts are there pleaded in detail. As required by Article 21(4)(a), the planning meeting in the Hotel Vitez, specifically alleged. At least Ljubicic is on notice of the material facts underpinning the charges against him. A privilege denied to Mr. Kordic. Judged by the governing legal tests erected by the Kupreskic appeals judgement and by the other cases elaborating the Tribunal's jurisprudence in this area, Kordic submits that the indictment in this case, the amended indictment, is unacceptably vague. As a result, Kordic was subjected to juridical impressionism, a case constructed as we go along, to use the words of one of the Trial Judges, a moving target case, to use Kordic's words at trial. The Prosecution was permitted to mould its case depending on how the evidence unfolded, and this was unfair. It's incompatible with the fundamental guarantees assured to any accused by the Tribunal's Statute that he has the right to a fair trial. Let me turn now to Witness AT.

utterances.text: Do you think you can make it within the next five minutes or -- because it would be not helpful for all of us if you have to break your arguments on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
