utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you one question beforehand. Is the intention of the Defence -- you have shown us a number of slides -- to give to the Prosecution and to the Judges copies of the slides shown during your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We had hoped, Your Honour, that that would be the position of the Appeals Chamber because of the tremendous amount of information that comes before your eyes. We have prepared CDs with all of this information on it and they're available to be distributed to the members of the Appeals Chamber and the Prosecution, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We will discuss it during the break. The trial stays adjourned until 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Sayers, before you continue, could you please be so kind and provide the parties and the Bench with a copy of the US Supreme Court decision Banks v. Dretke, because apparently it's not in the book of authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Banks v. Dretke was attached as Exhibit number 1 to the response filed by Mr. Kordic in February of this year regarding the supplemental reply, regarding Rule 68. We would absolutely be prepared to provide additional copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's have another look. We tried to find it in the book of authorities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Happy to do so. Your Honours, let me turn to Witness AT, in some respects a central issue in Mr. Kordic's appeal. The importance of the evidence of this witness cannot be underestimated. It was central to the planning, instigating, and ordering convictions. The Prosecution has recognised the importance of this testimony in its written submissions. Very important evidence, extensively relied upon by the Trial Chamber, is how it was described in the Kupreskic oral argument. The consolidated respondent's brief filed in this case, the significance and consequence of Witness AT's evidence cannot be disputed or underestimated. And it's been recognised by the Appeals Chamber as well just a month or two months ago in the Blaskic, 4th of March 2004 decision. The Trial Chamber relied in the Kordic case on the testimony of Witness AT to convict Kordic for the crimes in Ahmici. Based upon the hearsay testimony of this witness -- as I've said, a man convicted of murder, a man who admitted that he had lied to his own Appeals Chamber and Trial Chamber, a man who tried to perpetrate a fraud upon this Tribunal. Based upon the testimony of this witness, the Trial Chamber reached these conclusions: It was entitled to draw an inference that Mr. Kordic was involved in the plan hatched at the meeting held on the 15th of April, 1993; that Kordic was associated with orders for killings and detentions; he thus would have approved of General Blaskic's orders to kill; and that these orders would not have been given without political approval from the local leadership. We submit that these findings are clearly erroneous. The chain of command within the HVO was completely uncontroverted at trial. We'll bring this up shortly. We've actually got the exhibits for the Trial Chamber. The chain of command was a conventional, vertical chain of command. At its pinnacle was the supreme commander of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban. He was the supreme commander. He was the president. I noticed in the introductory remarks by the Presiding Judge today that the Appeals Chamber is of the view that Mr. Kordic was the vice-president of the HZ HB. That in fact is not the case. He was the vice-president of the Presidency of the HZ HB. It sounds like an artificial distinction, but it really is not. The supreme commander of the HZ HB -- of the HVO was the president of the HZ HB. The president of the HZ HB also happened to be the president of the legislature, of which Mr. Kordic was one of the two vice-presidents. But the supreme commander had under him the Defence department headed by Bruno Stojic. Under the Defence department was the Main Staff of the HVO, headed at various times by Brigadiers Petkovic, Praljak, and Roso. Underneath the Main Staff were the four operative zones, each headed by its own commander; in the CBOZ case, General Blaskic; and under the operative zones, various commanders - brigade commanders, military police, and so forth. Did the chain of command operate in a vertical fashion? It did. The local political leaders played no role in any of the cease-fire negotiations. Here's an example in the cease-fire agreements that led to the conclusion of the fighting in April of 1993. D83/1 is an order from the supreme commander of the HVO, Mate Boban, to the HVO Main Staff in Mostar. On the same day, having received that order, the Main Staff issues orders to each of the commanders of the operative zones. And that's Exhibit D84/1. And on the same day, having received orders from his direct military superior, Brigadier Petkovic, in the case of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Colonel Blaskic at that time issued Exhibit Z715 to all of his subordinate brigades, including the 4th Battalion of military police, to cease-fire. So there you have it. Chain of command operates in the expected conventional vertical fashion, with no involvement of the local political leaders. And it's not clear from the judgement why the Trial Chamber concluded that local political leaders, or any input from local political leaders in this vertical chain of command actually occurred. Now, if I might request that we go into closed session for just -- or private session for just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As I've stated, the Kunarac appeals judgement emphasises the importance, central importance, of contemporaneous objections. Contemporaneous objections to the testimony of this witness were registered in writing and orally. Hearsay evidence is, of course, admissible under the law of this Tribunal. But it must be reliable evidence. The Trial Chamber is required to pay special attention to indicia of reliability, and ordinarily, hearsay evidence is entitled to less weight than direct testimony. Although admissible, it's rigorously scrutinised. In the sister Tribunal, the ICTR, it has been stated that such testimony is to be assessed with caution. Akayesu appeals judgement. Commentators have made the observation in the context of European Court of Human Rights jurisprudence that it would not be fair to convict an accused based solely on hearsay evidence, especially where the accused did not have the chance to confront and examine the witness. Now, who was the witness in this case? The witness in this case was actually Ljubicic and not Witness AT. And I've put the central testimony on this slide here. "I did not see him with my own eyes." This is as to Mr. Kordic. Didn't see him any time. "My knowledge comes from Pasko Ljubicic." Who, of course, Witness AT, with his professional background, at that time knew not to be available. Absolutely perfect insulation for the witness, attempting to buy a discount from his sentence, having fought in his corner 'til the last, having been unsuccessful in foisting upon the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber a perjured alibi defence, comes up with a story that is uncheckable because the declarant, Mr. Ljubicic, at that time, anyway, was not available. He was a fugitive from justice. What evidence was there of who said what at this central meeting? I've said before, I'll say again, it deserves emphasis. There was no evidence. No evidence from anyone who was there, but there was evidence to controvert it. Two of the putative attendees, or at least one of the putative attendees and one possible attendee specifically controverted the testimony of Witness AT at trial. One was Zoran Maric. We've put his testimony on the screen, TR27956. Never heard there was a meeting, was not at this meeting. What kind of a witness is Mr. Maric? He has no criminal record. He's a former president of the parliament of the Central Bosnia canton of the Federation. He is a currently member, I believe, of the parliament of the Republic of -- or the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. No reasoned decision was articulated by the Trial Chamber of why this testimony was rejected. The second person identified as a possible attendee was Jozo Sekic. We called him in rejoinder, just as we called Mr. Maric. He too denied: "I wasn't at the meeting. Furthermore, even though I was the president of the HVO civilian government in Novi Travnik, I never heard of any such meeting, and to my knowledge, no one from Novi Travnik was there." Again, it bears mentioning that the jurisprudence on this point is particularly important. Single witness, uncorroborated testimony, especially when it's hearsay, must be rigorously scrutinised. The Trial Chamber, according to the Kupreskic appeals judgement, must be particularly rigorous in the discharge of its obligation to assess the credibility of the testimony before it. And here, as the judgement says, there was no direct evidence supporting the account given by Witness AT of this meeting. It is literally uncorroborated hearsay. Now, the law of corroboration in this Tribunal is relatively well recognised. We fully recognise it. The testimony of a single witness on a material fact does not require, as a matter of law, any corroboration, and that's true. That's the general declaration of legal principle that governs this particular part of Kordic's appeal. But it's absolutely clear when the Appeals Chamber considers how other Trial Chambers and how other Appeals Chambers have actually approached this issue of the necessity of corroboration or the importance of corroboration, that the absence of corroboration in this case is particularly significant. Cases in which factual findings in other cases have been overturned are fairly legion in this Tribunal. For example in Delalic, factual findings were overturned by the Appeals Chamber, despite the burdens of persuasion on appeal that attend an appellant. In Kupreskic the Appeals Chamber noted that corroboration assumes greater importance when single witness testimony is involved. Here, even though the Prosecution tried to argue that the testimony of Witness HH was corroborated in some general details, the Appeals Chamber insisted no, that was not corroboration, because corroboration must be specific. It cannot be general. Therefore, the testimony of Witness JJ in Kupreskic was found not to amount to corroboration as a matter of law. As a result, the Appeals Chamber, as I've said, was fortified in its decision to dismiss the indictments or to acquit Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic because of defective indictments. In addition, the presence of the central testimony in that case, the linchpin of the testimony against them, was not found to be reliable. Similarly, Krnojelac, Vasiljevic, Krstic; factual findings overturned. We are fully aware of the jurisprudence that governs requests to this Appeals Chamber to overturn factual findings made by a Trial Chamber. The Aleksovski appeals judgement outlines those principles in paragraph 63. In Delalic, for example, the -- even though there was a huge amount of evidence about the evil actions of Delic and the numbers of times that he had been involved in beatings. As to a particular incident of beatings, the Appeals Chamber found that no reasonable tribunal of fact could have found on the evidence presented that he had participated in that incident. In Kupreskic, as I've said, even though the eyewitness presenting identification testimony was found to be confident and forceful, her testimony was not shaken in cross-examination, the same formula used in paragraph 630 of the trial judgement in this case, and I might add in paragraph 725 of the judgement insofar as Witness Y is concerned. Despite that, despite the fact that she had no criminal record, despite the fact that it was eyewitness testimony rather than hearsay, this was found not to be a sufficient basis upon which to found a conviction. There were inconsistencies in her prior statements. She had added new details in her testimony, not found in her prior statements, and that's very significant because, as the Appeals Chamber will know from comparing the prior statements of Witness AT to his trial testimony, he added details, added filigree, added items of information designed to impart a more credible aspect to what he had said at trial from what he had said in his prior statements. "New details supporting his claim," to use the words of the Kupreskic appeals Judgement. His story underwent, frankly, not a degree of development but an entire chapter of development. It was subject to elaboration and diversification, just like Witness Agnes in the Simic contempt judgement. The flip side of the analysis is in the Krnojelac case. There, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the commander of the KP Dom was acquitted of certain crimes connected with detention facilities, and the Appeals Chamber said wait a minute; this fellow was a commander of the facility. He walked by walls which were bullet pockmarked and there were bloodstains all over them. There's no way he couldn't be aware of the foreseeable risk that people were being mistreated, people over whom he had supervisory responsibility. Therefore, no reasonable trial Chamber could have acquitted him on that evidence. In Vasiljevic, a particularly chilling example of cold-blooded murder of people on their knees begging for their lives and shot to death, as I've said in cold blood. Nonetheless, even there on particular incidents of conviction such as prospective killings of workers from the Varda factory, no reasonable tribunal of fact, based upon the evidence presented, could have come to a conclusion of guilt beyond on reasonable doubt. Similarly with respect to Vasiljevic's asserted membership in the Lukic group. Again, uncorroborated testimony of Witness VG14. That alone is not enough. Most pertinently, in Krstic, here you've got an inference of mens rea from certain circumstantial evidence, and again, the Krstic appeals judgement is significant in this regard. You've got to have direct evidence of the specific mens rea, and if you don't, if you're relying upon the actions of the accused, which are subject to various interpretations, one consistent with guilt, one not consistent with guilt, the inference that has to be drawn is the one in favour of the accused. The evidence fails to establish the direct involvement of the Drina Corps in carrying out the executions and as such cannot be relied upon as evidence of Radoslav Krstic's direct involvement in assisting the executions. Similarly, the court rejected the very vague must-have-known formulation in that case because General Mladic had a homicidal plan and Krstic was one of his subordinates. Krstic must have known of the homicidal plan and therefore mens rea could be inferred. The Appeals Chamber appropriately rejected that vague formulation and, frankly, criticised the vague phraseology of the Trial Chamber's findings in that regard. It should be clear by now that despite the Trial Chamber's assertions that if General Mladic knew about the killings then Krstic must have been known, the Trial Chamber did not actually establish from Krstic's contacts with Mladic during the relevant period that Krstic, in fact, learned of the intention to execute. And that's exactly what we have here. The same principle of law applies to the inference involved in this case. Now, Witness AT himself was not at the April 15th meeting. He did not hear what the participants said. He could not give any testimony about that. He didn't see Kordic at any time. He didn't hear Kordic. He didn't speak to Blaskic. And apart from his testimony, there was no evidence that General Blaskic had given any orders to kill. This is the same situation as envisaged in paragraph 98 of the Krstic appeals judgement less than a month ago. This witness testified, as I've said, just over a week before the close of the evidence in this mammoth case. This witness was sprung on Kordic after, months after the close of his case in chief. This witness did not rebut anything that Kordic said. It did not rebut anything that -- any evidence that Kordic introduced. This witness was providing fresh evidence. And that, we would submit, was unfair right at the end of the trial. Prior appellate decisions in this regard: The Haskic decision in July of 2000. The Prosecution had a number of theories of Mr. Kordic's whereabouts on the 15th of April. One of them was that he wasn't really in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone headquarters. He was actually in Donja Veceriska, based upon the hearsay statement of a dead witness, supposedly, Midhat Haskic. The Appeals Chamber said that this was not sufficient as the only proof of the accused's presence in a particular time at a particular place. It would not be possible to convict Kordic on the basis of this statement alone if the evidence was uncorroborated. The next appellate decision was the one dealing with Rule 94 ter corroboration affidavits. Rule 94 ter has since been deleted, but it was very useful in this case. It actually saves a lot of trial time. We were able to introduce affidavits to corroborate facts directly, facts that were testified about in examination by witnesses here. The Appeals Chamber emphasised that proper protection of the rights of the accused is overriding, but for corroboration to exist in terms of the affidavit there's got to be a clear link between the fact described in the affidavit and the fact testified about in the direct testimony of the witness. General background does not amount to corroboration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel be asked to slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please slow down again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My apologies. I know I'm a notorious offender on this and I'll try my best to slow down. One month ago, as to a particular incident in the Krstic case, the Appeals Chamber noted, very pertinently, that it was hesitant to base any decision on Mr. Deronjic's testimony without having corroborating evidence. And as a result, the combination of the circumstances in that case, the Appeals Chamber was cautioned against relying on that evidence alone. One particularly poignant example of the role of corroboration comes from the Naletilic trial judgement, which we commend to the Appeals Chamber's attention. I've excerpted a series of statements or observations and rulings made by the Trial Chamber. In this case, the Trial Chamber recited the general rule; single witness testimony on a material fact does not require corroboration as a matter of law. Let's take a look at how the Trial Chamber actually approached this issue. Reports of members prepared by a particular battalion corroborated, so reliable. Particular evidence corroborated by the Rados diary, so reliable. Documents corroborate witness testimonies. Witness statements corroborated by Exhibit PP. ECMM and UNPROFOR witness testimony, corroborated by testimony of many eyewitnesses. And it goes on. Example after example of where testimony is accepted because it's corroborated. But what happens when testimony was not corroborated? There were two examples, and those are on the bottom of slide 180 here. Witness AF, who placed Naletilic in the role of a perpetrator of torture and mistreatment at the Sovici school was rejected because this testimony was not corroborated by other witnesses. Similarly, the Chamber finds that the testimony of a single witness that he was told about mistreatments at, I think it's Dobrkovici, actually, lacked sufficient probative weight for a finding by the Chamber. In Kunarac, the testimony of Witness AS that she was repeatedly raped by Kovac was corroborated by Witness FWS-87 and accepted. How could it not be under the appalling circumstances of that case? But the Trial Chamber said that as to the testimony of Witness FWS-48, there was no supporting evidence to dispel the Trial Chamber's doubts about the witness's testimony, and therefore not convicted based upon that. In Vasiljevic, the trial judgement had more or less the same sorts of observations. We've already gone over the Simic contempt judgement. Even grave suspicion is not enough to establish proof beyond a reasonable doubt; considerably more would be required before Mr. Avramovic could be found guilty. The same is true in the ICTR. We've summarised these on slide 184. Musema appeals judgement. The -- I hope I'm saying this right -- Ntakirutimana judgement and sentence of the Trial Chamber. Rutaganda, the Niyitegeka judgement and sentence. That is a particularly interesting case. In that case, Niyitegeka was found to have abducted a young girl, spent half an hour in his car with her, kicked her out of the car, shot her to death, and subsequently, based upon the hearsay testimony of a witness that this accused had supposedly raped the girl while she was in the car, the Prosecution asked the Trial Chamber to believe that the offence of rape had been made out. Notwithstanding the murder, notwithstanding the circumstances, the Trial Chamber said: That's not enough. That's -- uncorroborated hearsay testimony is not enough to establish that a rape has also occurred. The same is true in terms of the jurisprudential argument we're making at the ECHR. Jurisprudence: Hearsay testimony should be approached with great caution. If it's not corroborated, it's not enough. The Saidi case, drug trafficking case, stands for that proposition, as does Kostovski. And most pertinently, the Unterpertinger case, where there was actually a fairly significant amount of evidence in terms of police reports, medical reports, and divorce files, but the out-of-court statements made by two witnesses were the central feature of the conviction, and that was found to be insufficient to found a conviction. Now, let's consider what the Trial Chamber ruled in this case. Because I think the approach taken by the Trial Chamber is absolutely telling. Witness K: Testimony about what Mr. Kordic supposedly said in a TV broadcast; rejected. No tape produced, so the Trial Chamber can place no reliance on the hearsay evidence. Nura Pezer: No corroborative evidence; testimony rejected. Witness AC: Without support about what Mr. Kordic supposedly said in a TV conference, no reasonable -- no reliance could be placed upon that. The same with respect to Witness H, Witness AP, and Witness I. The only exception in this case, Witness AT. Judged by a different rule. Yet, the Trial Chamber admits that this witness could not bring himself to tell the full truth about his own involvement. What the Trial Chamber really meant was, well, he lied about what he was doing in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, and as the Appeals Chamber well knows, that's exactly what he did. He lied about what he was doing in that village on that day. Now, the lying alibi defence. The Trial Chamber observed that the defence of the alibi was withdrawn and was not true, and then immediately proceeds to the next proposition. With all due respect to the Trial Chamber: Not so fast. Let's think about that. The Trial Chamber appeared to try to draw a distinction between lies assertedly told by lawyers representing an accused and the accused himself. It makes no difference who told those lies, whether it was the lawyer or the accused, because the principle of unity of counsel and client is absolutely uppermost in this Tribunal. The principle of unity is fundamental to the process of this Tribunal is an argument made by the Prosecution itself, not once, but twice. December 2001; 6 of February, 2004. I might say that the December 2001 pleading was filed two months after the Prosecution's respondent's brief was filed in this case, where Kordic's argument was depicted as being an overstatement and an exaggeration. But there's no question. The principle of unity of identity between client and counsel is indispensable to the workings of the International Tribunal. So it doesn't make a difference who told the lie, whether it was his counsel -- whether it was his counsel or whether it was him. Could we have a brief private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You may continue, please, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Since my time is short, I'm going to truncate this discussion somewhat, Your Honours, but let me just turn to the first meeting. There are three meetings that the Appeals Chamber must focus on. The first is the asserted meeting of political and military leaders, followed by a second meeting of military commanders, followed by a gathering of military policemen in the TV room of the Hotel Vitez. As I've said, no one knows who said what because no witness was called, other than Brigadier Grubesic, who was supposedly present at the second meeting. He testified that he was not, that he had never heard of any such meeting. Now, the orders to kill, the central orders in this case. When were they given? Here's what the Trial Chamber concludes: Well, I conclude -- we conclude there were two sets of orders, orders to kill, orders -- military-aged males, and orders not to leave any living witnesses. We conclude that one was given in the first meeting of political and military leaders, but we're not sure about the second. Here's the key testimony, Your Honours, and there it is in the words of the witness himself: "Your Honours, the first time I heard of that order, that all able-bodied Muslims had to be killed, was something that I heard for the first time in the Bungalow." So how could the Trial Chamber conclude that the first set of orders must have been given at the first meeting, while the second set of orders, it couldn't be sure that it was given at the first meeting? There is simply no evidentiary basis whatsoever upon which the Trial Chamber could reach that conclusion. Furthermore, with respect to Mr. Kordic's whereabouts, there was evidence that he was actually present at his own headquarters on Mount Tisovac, where he returned after the press conference on the 15th of April, from Brigadier Grubesic. And we've summarised that evidence on slide 210. Which raises some important questions about the law of alibi in this Tribunal. When are you supposed to assert an alibi? You are supposed to assert it as soon as practicable, under Rule 67(A)(ii), but in any event, before the commencement of trial. How are you supposed to do that if the indictment doesn't contain an allegation of where you supposedly were at a particular time and what you supposedly did? You can't. But Kordic submits that the evidence established, at least a reasonable possibility, if he had been given a chance to assert an alibi having been given a reasonably detailed indictment and had asserted it, the evidence asserted -- established at least a reasonable possibility that he was present on Mount Tisovac as stated by Brigadier Grubesic. Just a few concluding comments with respect to Witness AT. There are tremendous inconsistencies between the prior statements he gave and between the trial testimony he gave. He stated in his first statement on the 25th of May, 2000, that there was a possibility that Kordic was supposedly present at the Hotel Vitez headquarters on the 15th of April, 1993. In his second statement -- actually, he said in his first statement - I'm sorry - "I do not remember mentioning Dario Kordic being present." That was what he said his first statement. That's all that he had to say in his first statement about Kordic's asserted presence at that time. In the second statement, this was elevated from that to, "It's possible that he was present at the meeting," and then at the trial, for the first time he said: "Well, Ljubicic told me he was present at this meeting." That's the only state of the evidence. "I was told by Ljubicic that he was supposedly present." As you can see, a degree of development from "I don't remember Kordic being present" to, "Maybe, it's possible he was there," to, "He was there." That's exactly the same kind of elaboration and diversification of the story present in the Kupreskic appeals judgement and the Simic contempt judgement. Other inconsistencies. I won't spend too much time on this. The witness's statement that he couldn't speak Croatian. "Even today I cannot speak Croatian," he said in his 17th of August, 2000 statement. And why? Because he actually issued an order in Croatian to the subordinate units of the Jokers that he commanded, Exhibit D348/1. And look at the date. The date of this exhibit was the 8th of April, 1993, one week before Ahmici. What did he say about this document? Well, it's fictitious, it's false, he said. It was planted. But at trial he recognised that the signature was his. Could we have a brief private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: For evidence to be admissible in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Please forgive my acceleration, Your Honours. I'm due to hand off to Mr. Smith in ten minutes and I can see him champing at the bit, so I'll try to move as quickly as I can. Reliability is the golden thread that runs through whether a document can be admitted in this case. This whole discussion concerns specifically Exhibit Z610.1. If the evidence is not reliable, how can it possibly be admitted in this Tribunal? Rule 89(C) demands that evidence be reliable. And whose burden of proof is it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel be asked to slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That it is incumbent upon any party to authenticate the documents it tenders upon complaint of the other party. And ironically, in direct examination of the very first witness called by Kordic in this case, that precise point was made in no uncertain terms, I'm embarrassed to say, to me. You've got to lay the foundation for evidence for it to be admitted. One good example of the problem caused by this is Exhibit Z437.1, noted in the judgement at footnote 1052. The Defence points out that this document is neither stamped nor signed, and even though no witness authenticated it, no one said it was a correct document, the one person to whom it was shown, (redacted) I don't recognise it and it doesn't look like a genuine document to me. But what does the Trial Chamber say? "We find it a genuine document there being no evidence that it is not, despite the evidence of a stamp and a signature." Your Honours, it's not the -- it's not the obligation of the Defence to prove that a document is not genuine. It's the obligation of the Prosecution to prove that it is if it tenders that document. Furthermore, if the Defence tenders a document, it's its obligation to prove that it's a genuine document, that it's reliable, of course. The Tribunal's jurisprudence establishes that reliability is the central component of admissibility, as I've said. We've summarised that. The Tadic decision says that documents can be admitted for a limited purpose, but if they're subsequently shown to be unreliable, then they can later be excluded. Kordic made precisely such a motion with respect to some of the -- two separate documents, Exhibit Z1406.1 and 1380.4, but that was a completely unsuccessful endeavour on his part. The 22nd of September, 2000 decision in this case establishes -- sets out the proposition that there is no legal basis for the applicant's argument that proof of authenticity is a separate threshold requirement for the admissibility of documentary evidence. That's in this case, and the citation was to Delalic. When you go back and take a look at the Delalic decision, it's true that legal proposition is cited. But there's absolutely no legal citation for it. There's no footnote, no authority cited. It's a pure ipse dixit. And with full respect to the Appeals Chamber, Kordic suggests that that, ipse dixit, is wrong for the reasons stated in the Galic trial judgement. It is indeed incumbent upon the party tendering evidence to prove that it is authentic, reliable, upon complaint of the other party. Furthermore, in this case, Rule 89(E) should be taken into account. The Trial Chamber had full power to require the Prosecution to come forward with some proof of authenticity. It did not exercise its powers under Rule 89(E), and it's hard to imagine a case in which those powers more appropriately exercised or invoked than in this case, where Exhibit Z610.1 was actually an important document and relied upon by the Prosecution. This is exactly the kind of self-propelling evidence that has the power to get to the Appeals Chamber or the Trial Chamber under its own steam, to use Judge Robinson's very appropriate graphic analogy in the Aleksovski dissent he filed in February of 1999. Other authorities supporting Kordic's argument comes from the ECHR and from other noted commentators. The Matogrosso report says the case of Allan v. The United Kingdom, would not be admissible in evidence because its author could not be found to vouch for its accuracy and be cross examined on its contents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- authenticity has featured. Two examples, Your Honour, in the Vasiljevic case. The Visegrad health centre records tampered with, not reliable, exactly like Z610.1. No one testified that the records were made contemporaneously. In that case, excluded. In this case they come into evidence. A name had been overwritten. "Lukic" had been overwritten with "Bogic." In this case, as we know, the entry saying "war diary 15 April 1993" had been overwritten by someone on the January 29th 1993 entry. By whom? Who knows. As you can see, we've highlighted on this slide where that overwriting occurs. That's the English translation. Exactly the same as in the Visegrad health centre records in the Vasiljevic appeals judgement. By contrast in the same case, the Uzice hospital records found to be completely reliable, but there was no evidence that they had been tampered with and inconsistencies were convincingly explained by witnesses. It didn't happen here, though. The Prosecution has not been shy about making the same sorts of authenticity objections that we ourselves made throughout the case. The next series of slides summarise Prosecution submissions, and you'll see again and again and again the Prosecution says, "We object to this document. Unsourced, unsigned, unsubstantiated. We don't know who wrote it. We have no opportunity to cross-examine. The provenance of the document is unclear, anonymously written, veracity can't be determined. Unsourced, unsigned." Again and again, in pleading after pleading. We agree with the Prosecution with respect to all of those objections, every one of them. In this case, the Prosecution has said: "Well, we object to any documents when we don't have the opportunity of challenging the authenticity or opposing their use," to quote the ECHR jurisprudence in the Allan case. And we completely agree with that too. The same is true in the ICTR. In fact, the Appeals Chamber in the Musema appeals judgement stated: "The party relying on a document must establish that it has sufficient indicia of reliability." That's where the burden of proof lies, upon the party tendering the document. And here, Exhibit Z610.1 was subject to contemporaneous objections in writing and orally. The authenticating witness produced by the Prosecution couldn't authenticate it, Marko Prelec. With respect to the overwriting, he said, "I have absolutely no idea who did it." He didn't know who the duty-officer was. By the way, nor did Witness AT. And given the location of Witness AT's office, his inability to identify the duty-officer is particularly significant. Mr. Prelec said, "I have no idea who wrote that entry in the middle. I wouldn't know where to start." Witness AT: "Parts of it have been faked." The Prosecution's own witness says parts of the document that it tendered into evidence, after the testimony of this witness, had been faked. So parts of it were unreliable. Brigadier Grubesic, same thing. "Self-evident," he says. "Parts of it have been interfered with." The question was actually asked by the Judge, "Well, Where does --" one of the Judges, "Where does this document purport to come from? There's no indication on it. What you're seeking to put in evidence here has no indication whatsoever as to its origin." Exactly right. The Judge was completely right. So why did the Trial Chamber allow it in? Well, it's a document contemporaneously made, it carries its own authenticity, and it's signed by General Blaskic. Let's consider that for a minute and I'll end on this note. There was no proof by anybody that it was contemporaneously made. And in prior pleadings, the Prosecution has said, "The Prosecution is unable to confirm, with respect to a particular document, that the signature on the document belongs to Colonel Blaskic." So an objection is made by the Prosecution. "We don't know whether this document is signed by Colonel Blaskic or -- was signed by Colonel Blaskic or not." Okay. If -- who actually authenticated the signature of the document in this case, Exhibit Z610.1? No one. Here's the signature page, Your Honours. Take a look at it. Two signatures on there. Both purport to be those of General Blaskic. They're both different. Which one is his? Well, let's go to another document. That's a document containing the uncontroverted, the authentic testimony of General Blaskic, an order he signed on the 16th of April. Here are the three signatures, one, two, three. All different. Which one is his? Well, in conclusion, I can't tell you. The Trial Chamber couldn't tell you. The Prosecution couldn't tell you, and didn't try. How are you going to make the decision? And what's the law on that? It's pretty simple. The mere resemblance to other documents issued by the Crisis Staff is insufficient to determine authorship, according to the Simic sentencing judgement. No evidence to identify conclusively the signature of its president, Blagoje Simic. Therefore, the document is inadmissible. And that's exactly what the ruling should have been in this case. This document came into evidence at the last minute in the December -- 1st of December 2000 decision, a large quantity of last-minute document were excluded. Why? Because to admit them at this late stage of the case would be unfair and because the Defence would have no opportunity now of cross-examining anyone about this them. But this document was treated differently? Why? For no good reason. This document was subjected to precisely the same objections and no one authenticated it, the signatures were not authenticated, there was no evidence it was contemporaneously written. The authentication witness couldn't authenticate it. Witness AT said parts of it had been faked. How can you have any reliance in a document like that? But more importantly, for the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, who bears the burden of proof, of reliability of documentary evidence it tenders? It's got to be the party that tenders the evidence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask my colleagues: Are there any questions related to this chapter on fair trial, 68, and Witness AT, and document 610? Judge Guney, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, thank you very much for the submissions you've just made, which I followed with great interest. Having said that, I hope that you will agree with me if I say that the precise identification of certain areas indicated by your client, Mr. Kordic, is very important. In your fourth ground of appeal, Mr. Kordic states that the Trial Chamber found him responsible of a crime without having made the required factual findings. First, it appears pertinent to ask the question, that is, to specify the counts that he invokes there. I would be grateful if you could clarify this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Judge Guney, I would be delighted to answer the question, but with the Appeals Chamber's permission, I defer that to my colleague, Mr. Smith, who is prepared to answer that question specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think Judge Guney agrees. Judge Weinberg de Roca, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, as to the authenticity, has Mr. Blaskic been asked if it is his signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Judge Weinberg de Roca. Nowhere during his testimony, nowhere during the appeals hearing, no evidence whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Mumba, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel, for elucidating the points, factors, regarding the rule on practice of disclosure by the Prosecution. Do you accept the assertion that, in spite of the rigorous provisions and the pronouncements by various Trial Chambers and Appeals Chambers on this obligation by the Prosecution, that in any event evidence in the public domain is available to all, including the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think the Judge is asking whether access to open-session material may somehow alleviate the obligation of the Prosecution to disclose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Our position is that it does not. If the material is available in open session, it's got to be disclosed as soon as practicable. The rule means what it says. It does not need to be rewritten. That provision is very important. It does not need to be deleted from the Rule. And here's why: In our trial, we experienced extraordinary delays in obtaining access to portions of the open-session testimony of the general. I'm not confident even today that we ever got it all. Pieces of it were produced over a very protracted period of time, in no particular order. The numbering of pages made it extraordinarily difficult to match pieces up with what we had been given, because occasionally we were given LiveNote transcripts, occasionally unofficial transcripts, occasionally official transcripts. So I have to say, it's extraordinarily difficult to be confident to say that we had access to it all. Today, we have access to it all. It's all on the Internet, but it was not available that way at trial. And that was why it was extremely difficult to follow. But even if it had been, we should not have been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. subject to those huge delays in getting this material ourselves when it's the obligation of the Prosecution to disclose exculpatory material as soon as practicable. And let me just conclude by saying this: This was a case where the Prosecution was seeking a life sentence against our client for command responsibility under Article 7(3). Think of this: The testimony of the military commander of the entire area that our client had no military responsibility was withheld from us, never disclosed. When did we ever get a disclosure of the open-session -- sorry -- of the open-session testimony of the general? Never. And that's the same with Witness C1 in Kupreskic, the 14th of July 2000 testimony of this witness. When did we -- when was that disclosed to Kordic? Never. And as I've said, the closed-session testimony of this witness, which actually spanned a very considerable portion, 426 pages, was disclosed to us in three stages. The first was on the 23rd of May, 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the other details were given in your main submission. I just wanted to follow up that notwithstanding your submissions that the amended indictment was still not clear, it didn't specify the allegations, some of which the Trial Chamber had difficulty with in making findings, notwithstanding that, don't you accept, Counsel, that it is the duty of an accused person who has been served with an indictment, which makes, albeit broad allegations as to his conduct, to search, first of all in his memory, search where he is alleged to have been at various times in the indictment, and also search for possible material evidence in support of whatever his defence may end up being because he too has a duty, in a way, to defend himself and also to be able to effectively cross-examine Prosecution witnesses, right from the beginning of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The answer to your question, Judge Mumba: Absolutely. The accused has a duty to search his memory when he's asserted to have been present at a particular place at a particular time in an indictment, and to conduct the necessary investigations. But that's not what happened here. Don't forget, this amended indictment didn't allege that he was present anywhere at a particular time. It asserted a case of the broadest conceivable political/command responsibility against Mr. Kordic over a wide swathe of territory during a three-year period. And it's true, we specifically stated to the Trial Chamber, that's the case we were directed to answer, that's the case we were told to answer. And that's the case we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Pocar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Counsel, I thank you for your arguments on several issues. There is one point on which I would like to be clear as to your submission, concerning the Witness AT, and that's the following: Although, in general, the testimony of one witness does not need corroboration per se, your point is, if I got it correctly, is that in this case, that testimony indeed did require corroboration to be admitted. Now, is that because it was hearsay evidence and that, in general, hearsay evidence would require corroboration of a single witness, or because, in this particular case, due to the fact that that witness was a witness that may have a certain interest in the case, it required corroboration?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think the answer to the question, Your Honour, is both arguments. Hearsay testimony, generally, has less weight than direct testimony. Does it require corroboration if it comes from a single witness? It does not. That is the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. We clearly recognise it. But consider the circumstances of this witness: Under the circumstances presented here, for all of the reasons stated in the numerous cases decided by the Trial Chambers and by the Appeals Chamber, looking at the testimony of a single witness, the circumstances of that witness's testimony have to reinforce the Appeals Chamber's confidence that that witness is absolutely true. If there are circumstances which jeopardise that confidence, then the requirement for corroboration elevates in importance considerably, and in no case more than this one. As I've said, I'm not aware of any case in this Tribunal where any conviction, let alone so many convictions, have been based upon the uncorroborated hearsay testimony of a single witness, especially a witness like this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Now, the point you make appears to be conceded by the Trial Chamber in the judgement, and indeed, in paragraph 630, the Trial Chamber looks at corroborating evidence. Finding it in circumstantial evidence. Now, is that your point, that for the purposes of corroborating testimony of a single witness, hearsay witness in these circumstances, the reliance on circumstantial evidence is not enough, in general terms, or are you challenging the value of the circumstantial evidence relied upon by the Chamber, or both?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To answer your questions directly, Judge Pocar, we make a variety of arguments, but the most important ones are these: The law of corroboration in this Tribunal is that corroboration of the general circumstances of the witness's testimony is not enough. The corroboration has to be focused specifically on the material fact asserted by this witness. Now, the material fact asserted by this witness was Mr. Kordic's asserted presence at this putative meeting, a meeting -- well, now, what corroborating evidence is there relating to that? There is none. Not any evidence, and I don't think that would be contested by the Prosecution. What the Trial Chamber tried to do was to string together a set of inferences and said: Well, we can -- you know, what happened later in the day tends to show that what -- that the version of events told by Witness AT has validity, the sequence of the orders, things of that variety. That's not direct corroboration. It's not corroboration at all, actually, under the law of the Appeals Chamber. And that's one of the points we are making. And secondly, the importance of the requirement for corroboration, I rely upon my previous discussions of that particular subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Now it's quite clear what the point is. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As a follow-up: I think we are all aware that the Trial Chamber warned itself, in paragraphs 619 through 630. Would you, finally, come to the conclusion, and for what reason, that no Trial Chamber of fact could, based on the conclusions and the circumstantial evidence described in these paragraphs, could come to the conclusion that the Trial Chamber was satisfied that Mr. Kordic was present at the meetings of politicians?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With respect to that question, that's a fairly easy question to answer, I believe. What corroboration was there of the material fact about which this witness testified, which was, A, that there was a meeting. Nothing but his own unvarnished word. We had two rebuttal -- rejoinder witnesses who controverted this witness, both no criminal records, both men of substance. Second, that orders to kill were issued at this meeting. What possible basis was there for that conclusion? No reasonable tribunal of fact could have reached that conclusion beyond reasonable doubt, because there was no evidence to support it. Then thirdly: What evidence to support that version of events came from any of the other 240 witnesses in this case, 31 transcript witnesses, hundreds of witness in four other cases, thousands of exhibits in those cases and in this case, and, ironically, Exhibit Z610.1? In fact, the Trial Chamber I think reminded -- interrupted me during my cross-examination and said the witness will be able --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel be asked to please not to speed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sorry. Of a meeting between politicians and military leaders. So, quite simply, there is actually no corroboration of the material fact rather than the general circumstances of this witness's testimony, and under those circumstances, especially given the, dare I say, baggage of this particular -- that this particular witness carried, no reasonable tribunal of fact could have reached a conclusion that that meeting occurred beyond a reasonable doubt, let alone who said what at it. Because what is the evidence? Even this witness couldn't tell the Trial Chamber what it was. He didn't see Kordic, didn't hear him, didn't hear anyone at the meeting. That's the state of the evidence. We don't know what happened at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for these additional arguments. And now Mr. Smith, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will address, for the remainder of this session, chiefly the question of the findings and whether the findings are properly supported, a question adverted to earlier by, I believe, Judge Pocar. Before doing so, I will, however, say very briefly two things about the nature of the judgement: First, that what is charged in the amended indictment and found in the judgement is a broad form of persecution. You've seen the formulation before. Central Bosnia and beyond, extending to Zagreb, essentially persecution at the national level. What the Trial Chamber had evidence -- or adduced, advanced evidence to attempt to support, however, was a much narrower form of persecution, limited to attacks on villages in the Lasva Valley, and not indeed, really, as in many other cases, specifically aimed at forcible removal, but attacks on villages. And I will talk at greater length about that this afternoon. The second major thing about the judgement is that the category of intent involved for the joint criminal enterprise finding, in our judgement, is category number 3, and that is because the Trial Chamber infers, in paragraph 829, one of the crucial findings paragraphs, that Kordic shared the discriminatory intent, as I have on the screen for you. So it -- I'm sorry. If I said category 3, I meant category 1. Category 1 intent, in our judgement, and in our judgement, the joint criminal enterprise finding goes only to count 1. Counts 3 through 43, the finding in the -- on the subsequent pages of the judgement, paragraph 834, appears to be direct participation through planning, instigating, or ordering, sometimes perhaps committing, but very difficult to determine, based on the language used by the Trial Chamber in specific cases. Let me turn, then, to this question of findings. Were proper findings made by the Trial Chamber for each element of each crime, each count, each location, and each date? The short answer to that question, Your Honours, is no. And two things follow: Number 1, the convictions must be reversed on these grounds alone. Number 2, the Trial Chamber's decision cannot qualify as a reasoned decision. The first issue one of substance, the second issue one of procedure. Now, in an attempt to respond to Your Honour's request on this point of findings, we have prepared a tabular analysis of the findings by count, with the elements of each crime down the left side of the table. And I would like to pass those out at this time, if we could have assistance. And with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'd prefer to see it before making any decision, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could it please be passed first to the Prosecution

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have leave to explain it while the counsel is examining it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. In the interests of time. We have set out the elements for Article 7(1), individual participation, that is, committing, ordering, instigating -- planning, instigating, or ordering, and for Article 7(1) under the joint criminal enterprise theory. And we have then set out along -- those elements down the left side and the alleged locations along the top of the table. We have then also set out the elements for each count individually on a separate page or pages, with the elements down the left side and the villages alleged in the indictment for each specific count along the top of the page. Then we have filled in this matrix as best we could, indicating where we submit a finding was made; where we submit, with blank, there was no finding made; and commenting on the nature of the finding. Now, at this point, I don't know whether the Prosecution is ready to take a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If it will assist the Court, of course, and if the Court feels inclined to receive it. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated.
