utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is intended as an aid to argument, as the rest of the slide presentation is, and it was prepared expressly as the result of a suggestion during the pre-trial process for a very complicated set of conclusions and findings in the opinion, and I simply intend to argue the main conclusions about the findings in answer to Judge Guney's question based on the analysis that is in this document which then the Appeals Chamber and the Prosecution can examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. If it's in support of your submissions, and indeed it's true, in preparation of this appeal hearing. Of course, and I didn't ask to go through count by count but to be very detailed, and I think we all have to be very precise on the arguments to be found or not to be found in the judgement, and therefore, I think there is nothing wrong if you continue this way and then let's ask afterwards the Prosecution whether there are any objections or not and maybe only tomorrow. Let's wait and see. Please continue and, in general, we had only already one request by the Prosecution that it might be that Prosecution needs a little bit more time. If you need a little bit more time, it's no problem. It's better to be more precise than to be more fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Let me proceed, then, by addressing the findings in this case, and in effect to answer the question put by Judge Guney. The Trial Chamber, as Your Honours will recognise, made conclusory findings in many cases. The Trial Chamber was wrong on reciting evidence that was said was advanced by the parties. They did that at great length, the Prosecution on the one hand, the Defence said on the other hand. Then they had a tendency to append to that long recitation of evidence very short, brief paragraphs in which their own findings were asserted. Those were generally short, sketchy, conclusory, and did not disclose the reasoning of the Trial Chamber nor provide any real explanation either to Mr. Kordic or to the Appeals Chamber of the basis on which the conclusions were reached. Let me give examples. There are no express findings in most cases in this judgement on most of the elements for most of the locations, et cetera. The best example may be paragraph 649 of the judgement. This constitutes the main set of factual findings on the main underlying crimes at the main locations. It deals with counts 3, 4, and 7 through 20, and it deals with the Lasva Valley villages, the heart of the case, Ahmici, Nadioci, Pirici, Santici, Vitez, Stari Vitez, and Veceriska. This is a seven-line paragraph which makes six key points. First, it rejects the Defence case out of hand; second, it says that the evidence clearly points to organised HVO attacks in these areas. The Defence can agree to this. There were, in fact, HVO attacks, simultaneous ABiH attacks, in our submission. But this does not say that these attacks were against civilians or in any way illegal. They were military actions and this sentence says nothing more. It says that its findings must be seen against the background of the 15 April 1993 deadline, but that is an assertion which is belied by the finding in the Naletilic trial judgement at paragraph 23 that there was no deadline as such as of 15 April 1993, as the Trial Chamber relates. Second, the Trial Chamber says that its findings must be seen against the background of the wider attack on Vitez and the Muslim villages of the Lasva Valley. But this is precisely what is at issue in the finding. This is circular, to see the finding in light of the matter at issue in the finding. Then the Trial Chamber simply lists counts, lists localities, the seven villages, and then makes an attempt to bridge over its lack of specific findings by saying "The underlying offences are made out." That phrase "made out," in gross with no reasoning. That's all. No express findings, much less reasons, for all of the multitude of necessary findings as to elements and counts and villages in that matrix encompassed in that one generalised statement. But let's go beyond this one example to other examples in the judgement. There are, for example, no express findings on the Article 5 general elements that I could find in the opinion. There is no express finding that there was an attack on a civilian population squarely addressed. There is no finding that there was a widespread attack squarely addressed, or a systematic attack squarely addressed. Another example: There are no express findings of crimes -- that crimes, relevant crimes, were committed against "civilians," or against "civilian objects," or against "protected persons." And this matters, because in detention, they simply say "Bosnian Muslims." That's the quotation. Bosnian Muslims were detained. They take no position on whether they were civilians or protected persons or combatants or whether the defendants couldn't tell the difference at the time of the detention. There is also no express finding of discriminatory basis for each of the underlying persecutory attacks which, of course, are here, these attacks against villages which are charged individually also as crimes in counts 3 to 43. There is no express finding, for example, in count -- as to count 4 that the damage was "extensive" to civilian property. There is no express finding for count 38, that the damage at the relevant locations was "large scale," that it was "not justified by military necessity," or that it caused "grave consequences to the victim." There was no express finding as to counts 21 and 22, as I just indicated, that it was civilians or protected persons that were detained, simply a finding that it was Bosnian Muslims, undifferentiated. No express findings for count 39 that there was appropriation with intent to permanently deprive the victim, and no finding that what the victim was deprived of had sufficient value that it caused "grave consequences" for the victim. This next example is particularly egregious. Paragraph 834(C), at the end of the opinion dealing with the individual crimes 3 through 43, finds Mr. Kordic guilty under counts 38 and 39 at a number of locations. But if you will look at paragraph 809, which backs up those findings for counts 38 and 39 in paragraph 834(C) and compare the findings, what you find is that there are 15 villages for which Kordic was convicted either under count 38 or count 39 or both which -- for which there is no necessary factual predicate finding in paragraph 809 because they are omitted by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 809. And these include Kiseljak, Visnjica, Gacice, Behrici, Svinjarevo, Gomionica, Gromiljak, Polje Visnjica, Rotilj, Tulica, Han Ploca, Grahovci, Veceriska, Donji Veceriska and Jajce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, may I interrupt you. We have to be extremely careful what this Appeals Chamber is seized of at this point in time. You should be aware in relation to count 39, that already the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 35 of the 98 bis decision of 6 April 2000 that in relation to a number of villages or hamlets mentioned by you, there was no case to answer. In addition to this, on the Status Conference the 6th of May, 2004, the Prosecution conceded that the Trial Chamber did not make necessary factual findings in relation to Vitez and Donja Veceriska. So therefore, we should be extremely careful what we are still seized of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed. You're exactly right, Your Honour. I have tried to be, and Your Honour should check my list against both paragraphs 809 and paragraph 834(C) and these other dispositions to make certain that I have it right and carve it down if I have missed something. As I indicated earlier, this is very complicated, and we have been responding as rapidly as we could to Your Honour's request. There is no finding at all as to Kordic's -- no express finding as to Kordic's mens rea as to counts 3 through 43 for Kiseljak villages, Novi Travnik, Busovaca, and Merdani. There is no express finding of Kordic's mens rea as to counts 3 through 43 for Ahmici, any of the other Lasva Valley villages, Ocehnici, detention offences, counts 38 and 39, and count 43. The only express finding on mens rea at all in the opinion relates to count 1, persecution, in paragraph 829 of the decision where it is found that Kordic was "acting sharing the discriminatory intent" of the joint criminal enterprise, the basis for our assertion that the conviction rests on a category 1 offence. There are also imprecise and inconclusive findings in many cases. For example, and I will simply list several, paragraph 586 relating to Busovaca. Kordic is said to be "implicated in" the attack as a "leader exerting both political and military authority." From this finding, it is not possible to determine whether the Trial Chamber meant that he committed the offence because he was present in Busovaca during the fighting and he was not present at most of these locations for most of these events. Was it therefore direct commission they had in mind? Did they think that he planned it or that he instigated it or that he ordered it? One doesn't know, and as I will argue subsequently, there isn't evidence in any case in any of those situations. Paragraph 631. Kordic "associated with" the giving of an order. Again, imprecise, inconclusive. Paragraph 669, Kordic "involved in" attacks because "associated with" the orders. Paragraph 726, Kordic "associated with" the giving of orders. And paragraph 800, "Bosnian Muslims" found arbitrarily imprisoned without, as I indicated earlier, distinctions made as to the relevant legal categories of person involved. Thirdly, besides lack of findings altogether or conclusory, and the second category I just covered, imprecise and inconclusive findings, there are inconsistent findings in the opinion. Paragraph 576, Merdani, for example. Evidence found by the Trial Chamber to be insufficient for finding an attack on either civilians or civilian objects at Merdani. Yet they found the evidence sufficient for count 38, wanton destruction, and that in fact was based simply on evidence by a witness who saw Merdani being shelled from a distance. No other evidence as to any of the necessary elements of that crime. I have already mentioned the inconsistency between paragraphs 809 and 834(C) and the list of villages. In paragraph 842, Kordic is held responsible for detention crimes in areas for which he had "political responsibility," but he had no -- there's evidence that he had no such responsibility for Kiseljak, and even Prosecution witnesses agreed that he had no political authority in any real sense in Vitez, and that eliminates the necessary predicate for detention findings at every location except Kaonik in Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you again. On the transcript it reads in paragraph 842. 842 is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It should be 802, Your Honour. Thank you. One other potential inconsistency I will mention. Should the persecution count be upheld, which Kordic argues strongly it should not be, but should it be, then counts 7, 10, and 21 become cumulative under the recent case law of the Appeals Chamber, because they are crimes, individual crimes under Article 5 also charged as persecutory acts, and if they are found as persecutory acts to uphold the persecution conviction, then the Krstic appeal judgement paragraphs 230 through 33 indicates that they are cumulative. There are a number of legal conclusions in the judgement which are not backed up with factual findings, and Your Honours have discussed several in the pre-trial process. One in particular additional, however, that I would mention. In paragraph 669, Kordic is found "involved in" the April attacks on all of the Kiseljak villages for which he was alleged to be guilty in April in Kiseljak, because of course there are two time periods for Kiseljak, April and June. And the chief basis for that holding is an order by Blaskic, which the Prosecution argues inferentially refers to Kordic, but that order applies only to the village of Gomionica, yet it is used as the basis for holding Mr. Kordic guilty as to all of the other villages in the Kiseljak area in April. These, then, are the chief arguments I would make from the table. There are also a number of findings. In the interests of time I will not go over them, but Your Honours should look carefully at them, where the finding is only by inference and stated by the Trial Chamber only to be by inference. The plan, the joint criminal enterprise for a campaign of persecution is only an inference circumstantially arrived at. Kordic's intent, sharing the discriminatory intent, in paragraph 829 is only an inference circumstantially arrived at. In short, necessary findings were not made. They were not properly made. They were inconsistent in many cases. For this reason, in our judgement, when you look at the matter count by count, not a single count survives as a substantive matter. And secondly, this judgement is not a reasoned opinion. It does not give Mr. Kordic the notice he is entitled to on appeal to deal with the case as reasoned by the Trial Chamber and the convictions against him, and it does not assist the Appeals Chamber in its effort to take a hard look, as it now does, at judgements on appeal in order to prevent invalidity of convictions, prevent the omission of reversal where there is an invalidity in the conviction, and to avoid a miscarriage of justice. I propose now, Your Honour, to turn to the main substantive errors by the Trial Chamber in its evaluation of counts 3 through 43 and then of count 1, persecution, which I will tackle in the next period. First, I would like to set out but very briefly the nature of the Trial Chamber's errors to make clear that we are not simply re-arguing our case below. And if you will look at the slide material now, you will see that the first type of error we complain of at various locations in our briefs and in arguments is that either there was no evidence at all for a finding, there was no reliable evidence, or that there was no sufficient reliable evidence. Secondly, we sometimes believe that the Trial Chamber failed to take into account critical evidence, and I am omitting the examples in the interest of time. Third -- let me go back a moment. The Trial Chamber sometimes made erroneous evaluations of the evidence. And finally, there are many categories where there were other reasonable inferences available on the facts on a particular issue and the Trial Chamber failed to take the inference most favourable to the accused, which is an error both -- that is an error of law and involves an error of fact on the grounds that no reasonable Trial Chamber should have done that. All of the errors we deal with go to essential findings on essential elements of the crimes at various locations and under various counts. Thus they all demonstrate a miscarriage of justice, if we are correct, as well as the invalidity of the conviction involved. I turn next to the core of all of the counts, both persecution and involving the individual crimes, and that is the allegations of illegal attacks, HVO military attacks on villages. These are the basis both of the individual crimes and, therefore, a fortiori, of the persecutory acts. The central legal issue involved in these attacks is, in fact, whether or not they were directed against legitimate military objectives and did not cause civilian losses clearly disproportionate to the military objectives achieved, because they are military attacks by soldiers. And the first question is: Was this a legitimate attack against a military objective? Or, on the contrary, was it, as the Prosecution alleges, an attack directed primarily against civilians or civilian objects, depending upon the relevant count, in which case it was not an attack against a legitimate military objective. If these -- if these were legitimate military operations without disproportionate civilian damage, then they were not war crimes, nor were they persecutory acts. In short, even before the mid-1993 fighting, the Muslims - and I'm now talking about the general context of this fighting - the Muslims controlled much of the four Central Bosnia municipalities in which the Trial Chamber found Croat persecution. From June 1993 on, the Muslims controlled virtually all of the municipalities of Central Bosnia except for four small Croat pockets, one of which, Vares, subsequently fell in the fall. The outnumbered and surrounded Croat community in the Vitez, Busovaca and other Croat pockets - the other two - suffered greatly in the winter of 1993-1994, and came close to complete defeat before they were saved by the peace agreement in the spring of 1994. It is important, and I emphasise, it is important to consider at the macro level the military context in asking one's self the question of whether it is plausible, it is reasonable to believe that the Croat community and its institutions in Central Bosnia, if you adopt the narrow view of the persecution allegations and finding, would have set out to persecute the much more numerous Muslims that surrounded them and cut them off from the rest of the Croat community in Herzegovina. In short, Your Honours, this is Central Bosnia. What may have happened in Herzegovina is one thing. The question you are faced with is the plausibility of a criminal plan, a joint criminal enterprise for a plan of persecution, a campaign of persecution in Central Bosnia by this community. It just doesn't add up before I even start talking about the specifics. And I now want to turn to the first set of villages I will deal with, and I will now deal with several villages and with the detention and destruction of religious objects findings for the remainder of the hour, Your Honour. So let's turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If need may be, please tell us. We could also change the schedule that you can continue until 3.30. This would make no problem at all. We don't want to interrupt you unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Will that throw us off schedule thereafter, Your Honour? Because I have -- the reason I ask is I have, obviously, another 30 minutes, from 3.30 to 4.00, to deal with persecution and mens rea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's up to you to decide what fits best in your programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The short of it is if it is extra time, I will take it. If it is a rejuggling of time, I will take the break at 3.00 and begin the discussion on persecution and mens rea at 3.30, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So I take it then I shall stop at 3.00. Let's take the village attacks. Now, Mr. Sayers has already dealt with Ahmici and the chief evidence at Ahmici, and I'm going to deal with Nadioci, Pirici, and Santici, and then I'm going to deal with other villages. And I do this in each case by listing the substantive offences that are at issue so that that is clearly in mind, then examining the Trial Chamber judgement and its reasoning. I will not repeat this orally and I sometimes don't repeat it in slides, this business about the reasoning, because it's the same in every case. The role is as a political leader. The evidence is, in paragraph 834, as to the individual counts, the Trial Chamber simply throws up its hands and says we rely on the evidence already referred to as to persecution for findings for individual crimes, and I will not dwell on that each time, nor the fact that they generally reject the Defence case out of hand. I will also not dwell each time on the background cited by the Trial Chamber, which I've already addressed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So let me turn immediately to the evidence. In each of these cases, after discussing the Trial Chamber's judgement, I go to the evidence. First the convictions, then the Trial Chamber's judgement, then the evidence. These villages were guarded and defended. The Trial Chamber cited evidence on Ahmici but not as to Nadioci, Pirici, or Santici. They never cited any evidence that there was any massacre in these three associated villages on the same scale as in Ahmici. And this goes to Your Honour's inquiry in the pre-trial process as to whether there are factual findings to back up the convictions of Mr. Kordic for counts 7, 8, 10, and 12 of these villages in the judgement, and it is our submission that there is not. Now, despite the Prosecution's arguments in brief that Ahmici is a separate location from these three nearby -- is not a separate location from these three nearby villages, I simply refer you to the judgement, which treats these villages separately from Ahmici. So the evidence for Ahmici does not go to the situation in these three distinct surrounding villages. In candour, I must tell Your Honours that while not in the judgement, there was some evidence, not cited by the Trial Chamber, that military-aged men, some of whom who had been on armed patrol the night of the 15th and the morning of the 16th, were apparently killed in the fighting. There was some evidence, secondhand, non-specific, suggesting possibly some civilian casualties from in or around these villages. And this is important, because Your Honours must focus on whether there is actually evidence that there were civilians as opposed to combatants involved where there's an alleged crime. Now, in Ahmici there clearly were civilians. There's no question about it. And as executed, Ahmici was clearly a war crime. The issue there is what happened in the planning process, and we have argued Mr. Kordic simply had nothing to do with that and was not involved. I should say also, Ahmici was, as we've argued in briefs, a very strategic location. Notwithstanding that, the attack, as executed, did constitute a war crime. Now, there is notified as to Kordic's involvement in these Nadioci attacks, Pirici and Santici. There is no evidence that a crime was planned for these three villages at the -- any putative April 15th meeting. Even if there were evidence that there was a crime planned as to Ahmici, not so as to this and all of the other Lasva Valley villages. In short, then, after coming to conclusions from the evidence, the question is: What are the Trial Chamber errors? And we've tried to be precise about this in each argument. No recent decision, which I've already addressed and I won't repeat. No proof beyond reasonable doubt of Kordic's involvement as to these villages, because there is simply no evidence that he planned any crime at these villages. And I summarise that on the slide. No evidence that he ordered any crime. No evidence that he had any authority to order any perpetrator, and no evidence of any deliberate order by Kordic in execution of which any perpetrator committed any crime at these villages. Indeed, no evidence of any intent or desire, much less even awareness that there was going to be a crime. And this is true once you get outside Ahmici and that meeting relating to Ahmici and all of the locations. And of course, it's our submission that that evidence is insufficient as to the meeting in Ahmici itself and Mr. Kordic's involvement. Likewise, no evidence of instigation, simply lack of evidence. Where is Mr. Kordic in all of this? And no proof of his mens rea. And I turn to Vitez and Stari Vitez. And I am going to cover this only very summarily. The story here is there is no evidence linking Mr. Kordic to the Vitez, Stari Vitez fighting, no evidence that he had any mens rea as to that fighting, and I should note that the damaged mosque in Ahmici -- in Stari Vitez was being used by a sniper. That's what the evidence shows. And I turn now to the Novi Travnik situation. Now, in Novi Travnik, you have heard already something about, and there's been a good deal about in the briefing, the question of who was in charge at Novi Travnik. And because Your Honours, I think, are aware of that issue and up on it, I am not going to deal with it right now. Rather, I'm going to deal with a very important issue. You will notice there are only two counts involved at Novi Travnik, count 38 and count 39, wanton destruction and plunder. And in order to find that there was wanton destruction, there has to be evidence. There is evidence that during the conflict, a number of Muslim-owned buildings were burned or demolished. That evidence, however, is - and cited by the Trial Chamber - seems to be secondhand. The gentleman simply reports that it's his understanding that this took place, and it does not establish in any case anything other than that he says those buildings were damaged. It does not establish that the HVO troops caused any relevant damage, does not establish that that damage was in the zone of the fighting or not in the zone of the fighting. Indeed, it appears not to be in the zone of the fighting, because the fighting ran through the middle of town, and this appears to be elsewhere. And it does not show the damage to be large scale. In short, as with so many of the findings, virtually all of the findings, when you dive down and look at the specific facts and the specific elements, it evaporates. In short, Novi Travnik was an episodic flare-up over control of the strategic military arms factory during which there simply isn't adequate proof that there was -- there were violations of all of the elements of counts 38 and 39, whatever you think about Mr. Kordic's participation, and we know that he was not in command. I will go on to Busovaca and Merdani. Our argument in Busovaca is that there was an attack. There was fighting in January, no question. The issue is whether there is proof of war crimes and of whether Kordic is linked to any specific proved war crime and whether he had mens rea, and there's findings and evidence of his mens rea as to any specific war crime. The conclusion that there were war crimes in Busovaca rests on several bases: first, the testimony of Witness AS; secondly, an UNPROFOR report; thirdly, the Trial Chamber cites the 20 January alleged ultimatum, and it draws the conclusion from these three events that the HVO attacked the ABiH using the ABiH attack the day before in Kacuni as a pretext. And the Trial Chamber concludes that there was only "some defence," minimising the evidence and saying the Croats attacked first, and the Muslims, there was just some defence. Well, let's look at the facts. As to Kordic's culpability, not the question of war crime now but the question of Kordic's culpability, the Trial Chamber cites three main pieces of evidence: first, a tape recording of a telephone conversation between Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic; secondly, miscellaneous military documents mentioning Kordic, involving Kordic, from which inferences are argued; thirdly, testimony that Kordic at times during that fighting was where any sensible would have been, which is in a basement in the headquarters of the units involved in the PTT building, in the basement office. The Trial Chamber also relies in a very unspecified way - again imprecision in analysis - on Kordic's alleged control over roads, but never says why that matters. And the Trial Chamber finds Kordic, as a result, implicated in the attack; and I indicated already, one simply can't know on what basis, whether as a committer, planner, instigator, or order -- person ordering. Well, let's take a look at the testimony of Witness AS. Witness AS testified - this was a Prosecution witness, their star witness at the end of their case - that Blaskic personally commanded the January military operations. Witness AS listed military actions at several locations in which he participated, but he gave no details as to those actions. He testified that his police unit never attacked civilians deliberately, that he never -- was never ordered to attack defenseless civilians, and that his police unit was never ordered to attack or set fire to Muslim villages. Witness AS never mentioned Kordic in connection with any of these military operations. Witness AS testified, in fact, that the person he interacted with was Ljubicic, his commander, who got his orders from Colonel Blaskic by telephone, for reasons I will indicate in a moment. In short, Blaskic was the military leader, he said, and Kordic had political responsibility. Let's turn now to the -- let's me go back a moment. I'm sorry. Witness AS did mention the word "cleansing," and despite all of this other testimony, that's what the Trial Chamber seized on, that word "cleansing" in the English translation. That word, if you examine the transcript carefully, was placed in the witness's mouth by a leading question from the Prosecution. That's the derivation of that terminology. And Your Honours had been through the question whether when one uses that term and in the military context one is talking about mopping up or urban fighting generally or whether one can really safely infer that this witness, who was simply responding to the question from the Prosecution's counsel, intended to say in complete contradiction to the rest of his testimony that his unit and he had engaged in a war crime in ethnic cleansing. Now, let's turn to the UNPROFOR report. That report is -- there is a contrary report, a contemporary -- that report, first of all, is from the Kiseljak headquarters, a higher level, removed somewhat from the action. And there is another ECMM report, Z454, that gives a more accurate assessment of the fighting. It does not blame the Croats, the way the UNPROFOR report does, and it does not cite the 15 January "declaration" as a causative factor for the fighting in Busovaca in January. Let's turn to that declaration. The text of that declaration says -- first of all that, declaration is designed to be an implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. If you look at the text, you will see on its face that there is no ultimatum. There is a proposal for on a reciprocal basis for separating and mutually subordinating these two forces that were on the same ground at the same time causing great difficulty which resulted ultimately in their getting into a civil war later on in April. The Croats, furthermore, agreed before the "deadline" ran to renounce and withdraw this alleged ultimatum. Furthermore, the fighting began at Gornji Vakuf on the 11th, and that's before the deadline ran. So Z390.2, that UNPROFOR report at headquarters, they just got it wrong. That January "declaration" did not result in the Gornji Vakuf fighting. Now, let me be very brief about the nature of the military actions here. The record is clear that there were extensive ABiH preparations around Busovaca. Troops concentrated, the area was sealed off from Kiseljak and stayed that way for the rest of the war. Most of the Muslim population left Busovaca right before the fighting, secretly. And just before the fighting, the ABiH captured 16 HVO soldiers up on the Busovaca plateau. As I said, they sealed off Busovaca and Vitez from Kiseljak, and they began the fighting on the 24th at Kacuni. Let's look at the evidence from the BritBat observers. Lieutenant Colonel Stewart and Major Jennings agreed that the Kacuni killings were the principal catalyst for the Busovaca fighting but not that they were a pretext as the Trial Chamber found. The fighting itself began early on January 25th, as reflected by the evidence, with shooting and shelling from all sides. The Croats then moved on the morning of the 25th of January to disarm 50 to 100 TO members, Muslim combatants, who were in fortified positions in and around Kalice Strane [phoen], which, if you look at the map, you can see is a Muslim area on a hill immediately overlooking the downtown area of Busovaca, threatening, almost by pistolshot, the downtown area of Busovaca. The Muslims were warned but they refused to surrender, and the fighting having commenced, the Croats attacked that community to eliminate that threat to the heart of Busovaca. And this is recorded in milinfosums and the testimony of Brigadier Grubesic. The ABiH attacked the Croats in Milovace [phoen], and there was fierce fighting on both sides, and I've provided citations. The 17th Krajiska Brigade attacked Javor, and I've provided citations. The attacks by the ABiH then continued for several days. Colonel Blaskic operated by telephone from Kiseljak, where he was cut off. On the question, then, whether there was a Croat attack and some defence, look at Colonel Stewart's contemporaneous diary and consider that, strategically, the Muslim objectives were to cut off communications at Kaonik and Kacuni and to isolate -- to cut the pocket in half, essentially, so that Kiseljak was isolated from Vitez and Busovaca. The HVO then counter-attacked, and these are the counter-attacks that Witness AS spoke about and participated in. Indeed, his unit did try to take Merdani on the 27th but failed. During this entire set of attacks, the HVO was greatly outnumbered in Busovaca. They were on the ropes. Lieutenant Colonel Stewart blamed the Muslims in his book and in his testimony. Major Jennings shared this view and said that the Muslims refused to discuss Kacuni. They were very uncooperative. And most importantly, Blaskic was caught out of position. Now, if this wasn't a Croat deliberate, planned Croat attack against the Muslims as a part of a campaign of persecution to be kicked off in January in Busovaca, why was Blaskic in Kiseljak when the fighting began when his headquarters was in Vitez? No responsible military commander plans an attack, a campaign of persecution, and then gets caught out of his headquarters when his plan goes into the operation. Yet this is not a fact that the Trial Chamber discussed. They basically ignored this, but it's very, very telling. Now, as to Kordic's role, the BritBat officers were told directly by Kordic that he had no military authority in this same time period. Blaskic himself said he was the commander on 1st of February and that Kordic had no military authority, as reported in an UNPROFOR report. There we go. And Kordic did take an active role in this fighting. No question about it. This was in his backyard. His family lived in Busovaca, and he was the senior political leader on the spot when Blaskic was caught off base. He spoke daily to the press, spent time in his office, spent time in this more secure headquarters, he was copied on some of the military communications, he did use his influence to try to help the HVO receive reinforcements. He had telephone conversations with Blaskic, but listen and read very carefully the content of that telephone conversation. It relates to an artillery attack, not a war crime. Kordic has to ask Blaskic to consider various military steps, and the text of that discussion makes it clear that the HVO officers would not obey Kordic. "I told him but he won't do anything without it." And I will get to that in a moment. There it is. I must conclude quickly, but the short of it is that Kordic tried on some occasions to meddle in artillery activities but that meddling was generally rebuffed. That is what the text of the tape reflects. That is what the documents reflect when you analyse them carefully, as we have done in the brief. I submit to you, therefore, that at Busovaca, there is no proof of specific war crimes. The Trial Chamber is wrong on the facts that the Croats attacked the Muslims is the beginning of a coordinated campaign of persecution when Blaskic was out of position, and in any case, Kordic participated as an active political leader would be expected to participate; in public statements, present in headquarters occasionally, trying to get logistical assistance, sometimes being copied on military correspondence with Blaskic out of position. But Kordic was not the military commander. He did not have responsibility for the fighting. There was, in any case, no war crime proved. And when you look at the facts after the event and you look at the Busovaca Joint Commission's report, it was the Croats who were most severely damaged, both in terms of personal injury and property damage during the Busovaca affair. I will rest on brief, Your Honour, on the issues involving the unlawful detention and the destruction of institutions dedicated to religion or education and begin after the break on the question of persecution and then mens rea.
