utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, much of what I have already said relates directly to numerous material, Trial Chamber errors, as to both the crucial persecution and the mens rea issues. I now turn to deal with each individually. I'm starting with persecution, and I am starting with the question of the adequacy of the indictment insofar as it relates specifically to persecution and specifically to joint criminal enterprise. And these are quotations similar to those that Mr. Sayers used this morning from the Vasiljevic trial judgement and the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber. The point is that the amended indictment is defective, in our submission, because it charges, number one, a broad, non-specific campaign of persecution; number two, as charged, extending to areas for which no specific evidence was offered, where Kordic had no political influence, and as to which Kordic was found not guilty. The Appeals Chamber has held that, as to -- now switching to joint criminal enterprise, that using the concept of joint criminal enterprise to define individual responsibility requires a strict definition of common purpose and that the persons within the group have got to be identified as precisely as possible. In short, the Krnojelac appeals judgement has established four requirements for the Prosecutor in pleading joint criminal enterprise. First, that he must plead the common purpose or design specifically. That was not done in this case. The language in the indictment, and I've cited the paragraphs, says only that Kordic, together with certain persons, did X, Y, or Z. There's no mention of common purpose or design there. Second, the Prosecution must specify carefully the purposes of the common purpose, and here the allegation is very broad and generic of a campaign of persecution. Must also identify as precisely as possible the principal perpetrators. But when you look at the amended indictment, you find that it charges, in a formulaic way, over and over, Kordic together with various members of the HDZ, BiH, the HZ HB, HR HB and their leaders, armed forces, and agents. Simply vague and non-specific. And fourth, the Prosecution must charge the specific category of joint criminal enterprise, or common plan, as it was then called, that they are alleging. Not done in the indictment or even in the pre-trial brief. Paragraph 26 of the amended indictment mentions foreseeability but not specifically in the context of the common plan for joint criminal enterprise, and foreseeability is relevant for many reasons as to various elements. Even if the amended indictment were read to have pled a category 3 joint criminal enterprise, that is not what Kordic was convicted on. Then there is a mismatch between the pleading and the conviction, because he was convicted of a category 1 joint criminal enterprise. Now, in dealing with persecution, what is alleged is a political military campaign of persecution, in itself a very vague concept. I've dealt with the military side at some length, and I will again briefly. I turn now to the political side. The Trial Chamber's judgement found Kordic criminally responsible for participation in this campaign of persecution for essentially two reasons: Due to his status and due to his role. Insofar as his status is concerned, they found that he was the political leader of the Bosnian Croats in Central Bosnia, but, of course, as Mr. Sayers has indicated, only a local leader, not engaged at the highest levels. And, of course, he was, as you would expect of any political leader during a time of military operations, associated with military leadership. That's not surprising and not per se criminal. As for his role, Kordic was said to have, as a political leader, participated in certain political events; the HVO takeover of the municipalities and certain military events, the attacks that I've already discussed. The accused, in terms of evidence relied on as to role. The accused's positions, relied upon by the Trial Chamber, are his positions in a political party. Not in the government, not in the military. Mr. Sayers has made these points. The evidence in the case, however, demonstrates, by the testimony of Mr. Vucina, who was an outstanding and credible witness, a representative in the House of Representatives of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and well placed to know the truth of what he testified to on the point I'm coming to, because he was the president of the Executive Committee of the HDZ BiH during the war. What he said was that during the war, during the period that this indictment deals with, the political party was dormant and inactive and that events were directed by and actions taken by the government and the military during that wartime period. Now I am going to turn to dealing with the political aspects of the charge of persecution, and I am going to begin by reflecting upon a statement by the Presiding Judge in this case. He said: "I hope this isn't going to end up as being a trial about politics." But it did end up being a trial about politics, and it did because that is the way the Prosecution pled the case and that is the way the Prosecution tried the case. Turning to the political events. There were two main sets of political events that the Trial Chamber focused on and that were discussed and dealt with in the evidence. One is the establishment of the HZ HB and especially its purpose. And this was at the national level, and that's what I will deal with first. Secondly, then there were - and I'll come to this - HVO attacks -- sorry, HVO take-overs of municipalities alleged, and I will deal with that as well. In fact, I will deal with each in turn. First, the purpose of the HZ HB. This is the national-level issues. Kordic, of course, found not to be involved in the national leadership. But nonetheless, the Trial Chamber concludes that the Bosnian Croat institutions intended to secede from the RBiH and associate with Croatia, and that is what we must examine. The conclusions of the Trial Chamber on this matter deal mainly with events during the earliest period covered by the amended indictment in the fall of 1991, and in fact some of them before the period of the amended indictment, although the Trial Chamber does mention a few events in early 1992. The Trial Chamber's analysis of these essentially historical and political matters, which we examined at great detail in our trial brief in an annex and in the brief itself but had no room to do in our Appeal Brief, has some critical and material errors. The Trial Chamber, for example, concluded that Mate Boban became president of the HZ HB the following month after Mr. Kljuic resigned. That is simply not the case. It concluded that the Croats took advantage of the Muslims in the gaining of weapons in the period when the JNA was leaving the facilities at the Slimena barracks. That, for the reasons that I've set out, is in error. The credibility of the Trial Chamber's grasp of the national political situation was fatally undermined by its gross error in concluding that Mr. Kordic was exercising power politically and became vice-president of the HR HB, the political successor to the HZ HB. Simply not the case. The Trial Chamber, as to this whole issue at the national level, failed to cite, failed to credit, in most case, the official documents that Kordic has cited, and the credible witnesses Kordic put on, stating and establishing, for example, that the Bosnian Croats advanced a legitimate political objective, that their institutions were only temporary, that they were independent of the -- they were not independent of the RBiH, never asked to be independent, never urged annexation to Croatia by force. They were not and never purported to be a sovereign government under international law, and there was a great deal of confusion about the use of the term "sovereignty," meaning sovereignty of a constituent people within a political community in the Balkans versus sovereignty in the international law sense, which they did not claim. The evidence establishes that there was no de jure discrimination, and it established no de facto discrimination. There was evidence that I want to pause on, however, and that is the Tudjman transcripts. Evidence put in by the Prosecution of the meeting in Tudjman's office on December 27th, 1991, which is said by the Trial Chamber to be incriminating. Nonetheless, it does not establish that even if secession was dreamed of at the early stages of the breakup, in the fall and winter of 1991, that it was intended to go forward then or to be done by force. It was to be considered only as a last resort. Tudjman told the Bosnian Croat leaders to negotiate with the Muslims in December of 1991. He never instructed that BiH was to be partitioned, never instructed that the Croats there were to secede at that time, never instructed or demonstrated any desire that the Bosnian Croats should proceed by force or threat of force. Notwithstanding all of this evidence, the Trial Chamber has found, with no explanation, that there was an intent to secede. But even if there were, that finding accords only legitimate political objectives. It is clear on its face that this finding can support no conclusion of either discrimination or persecution. It contains no finding of intent to use force, and even if it had, use of force to achieve legitimate political end is not a war crime before this Tribunal. Switching to the alleged HVO takeovers. This Tribunal, in language in several opinions, Judges have concluded that the forcible takeover of a city or town does not constitute a war crime or a separate claim under Article 5. And there is a great deal of evidence that I do not have time to go over dealing with the take-over in Busovaca, establishing point by point in our briefs that the allegations as to discrimination after the takeover cannot, in fact, be maintained on the facts, and we have argued that the take-over itself was a reasonable political response by the group that controlled the government at that time to the situation created by the Muslims in their attempt to take the weapons at the military barracks at Kaonik. And I'm now going to turn to mens rea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be appropriate? Judge Weinberg de Roca has a question. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: You have repeated that Mr. Kordic has been found responsible for areas where he had no political influence, and I would be grateful if at this stage you could specify in which areas you submit he had political influence and which are the areas which you submit should be excluded. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: He had political influence in Busovaca. Later, during the war, he had political influence in that region, that pocket, Vitez-Busovaca area. But in terms of political influence in Vitez, for example, in the spring of 1992, when there was a take-over, that was not his bailiwick, and it would take me a moment to find it and I may give it to you after I've sat down at some point, but there is Prosecution witness evidence to that effect. But he was completely cut off from Kiseljak. That was Ivica Rajic territory, and the evidence is clear on that matter. May I then proceed with mens rea, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Special care has to be taken with findings of criminal intent. The Appeals Chamber has taken the view that an inference of intent, when intent is inferred, it must be the only reasonable inference. The Krstic facts, dealt with by Mr. Sayers this morning, demonstrate that inferences from mere presence, inferences of shared intent from mere presence, even where the person was present at a meeting and therefore had knowledge of what was going on, are insufficient; there's got to be evidence of mens rea. I want to discuss briefly what the record shows about mens rea. From a brief examination of the facts, it is clear that there is no evidence that Mr. Kordic intended to cause Muslims harm, much less to cause their removal, because they were Muslims rather than persons in political or military opposition to him and his community in the conditions they both faced, not created by either community in Bosnia at that time. This is seen in his character, his words and writings, his actions toward Muslims, and his actions in support of peace. And we have outlined these in our briefs at some length. I will simply say that - and I want to underline - when all was said and done, at the end of the conflict, Mr. Kordic exercised leadership in having the political solutions adopted by the Croat community in Central Bosnia, who were not happy with what the deal that was being served up for them by the -- because the Croat community was dominated politically by people in Herzegovina. But Mr. Kordic took a lead, even at risk of his life, and in an official position aided in the implementation of the peace after it was achieved, and that is an extremely significant and telling point. I will conclude, Your Honour, by saying that the Trial Chamber applied 20/20 hindsight, circumstantial hindsight, on events, political and military, to conclude, to conjure up, indeed, a joint criminal enterprise and a campaign of persecution against Croats in Central Bosnia where there simply was none, and therefore, and that's why there's simply no evidence of it. This is an inferential case from political events that have other reasonable explanations, as we have briefed, and military events that have other reasonable explanations. In a context in which both communities were struggling with a situation, refugee flows, lawlessness, matters not created by them but which Mr. Kordic and other leaders in both communities had to deal with as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. best they could, and with the Serbs aiding, the two communities fell to fighting, and there were political and military events which we have explained. The reasonable inferences were ignored by the Trial Chamber that are favourable to the accused, and that's critical. The Appeals Chamber must rescue the credibility of this Tribunal and of the development and application of new and evolving use of international criminal law, in the eyes of history and in the eyes of the world, by being extremely careful with the application of the concept of persecution, to political and military events which have reasonable explanations and where there are reasonable inferences about the way persons behaved. And I am focusing on Central Bosnia. There was no joint criminal enterprise. There was no campaign of persecution in Central Bosnia. There was fighting. There were lots of bad things that happened. A plan of persecution by this minority community outnumbered, surrounded, simply doesn't add up. Dario Kordic was a responsible political leader in a very difficult time. He did the best he could. He did not have the requisite discriminatory mens rea that the Trial Chamber could only infer from political events and military events which he necessarily participated in in his role as a political leader. And he was not responsible for the crimes at Ahmici. And Mr. Naumovski will now deal with the three villages -- sets of villages that I omitted in my discussion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Any questions? Not the case. Then Mr. Naumovski, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. Can you just give me a moment to prepare. I am ready now, Your Honours. I do apologise. Your Honours, I will continue on, but I will discuss primarily the Kiseljak area and the events that took place there. It is the contention of the Defence, and you will see from the arguments that follow, that the conclusions of the Trial Chamber on the criminal responsibility of Mr. Kordic for the events in Kiseljak - and when I say "Kiseljak," I am referring to the entire municipality, as well as the town; that is, over ten villages and the town of Kiseljak - that the evidence is very tenuous, and, in our view, unfounded. Almost all the conclusions about the events in Kiseljak are summed up in paragraph 668 and 669, and paragraph 724 and 725 of the judgement. I have also prepared certain slides, and I hope that this will make it easier to follow my argument. All the evidence analysed by the Chamber boiled down to a single piece of evidence for each event, and I will tell you what events these are. There is no linkage with Mr. Kordic as far as the events in Kiseljak are concerned, let alone any visible elements of Kordic's mens rea. Mr. Kordic has been found guilty on counts 3 and 4, for the village of Rotilj, unlawful attacks on civilians, for April 1993; and for Rotilj, Tulica, Han Ploca, and Grahovci, counts 7, 8, 10, and 12. I will not read each count. Also, in relation to the town of Kiseljak and the villages of Svinjarevo, Gomionica, Polje Visnjica, Rotilj, Tulica, and Han Ploca, Articles -- counts 38 and 39. There are also the villages of Visnjica, Behrici, and Gromiljak, count 38; and count 43, which refers to the village of Han Ploca in June 1993. What does the judgement say about the events in April, April 1993? The Trial Chamber established, in paragraph 753, that the evidence does not show that Mr. Kordic had control over Kiseljak, because his influence and authority were concentrated in the Lasva Valley. In the same paragraph, the fact that Kordic was the leading political figure in Central Bosnia does not of itself establish that Kordic was involved in this offence outside his sphere of authority, and the attack was not part of any common plan or design to which he was party. The attacks in the Lepenica Valley, which starts about 25 kilometres away from the Lasva Valley -- and these valleys, as the Chamber knows, were completely cut off as of the 24th of January, 1993 -- these attacks, according to the judgement, as stated in paragraph 669, occurred two days after the attacks in the Lasva Valley. According to the conclusion of the Trial Chamber in paragraph 753, these attacks were part of a pattern of attacks on Muslims in Central Bosnia. I have to say, however, that the Trial Chamber concludes, in paragraph 753, that with regard to Stupni Do, the attack by forces which had come from Kiseljak were not part of an overall plan of which -- in which Mr. Kordic would be a participant, and Mr. Kordic was acquitted of this. As for the events in April, the judgement states that Blaskic's order of the 24th of September, that is, Prosecution Exhibit Z733 -- I do not wish to enter into problems of identification because this may or may not be Blaskic's order, because he did not sign it himself, but everybody refers to it as such, and so I will too. And in paragraph 668, it states that Blaskic informed the leadership of the HZ HB of everything. I have to say that the original document in Croatian is different because the original states: We informed the very top leadership of the HZ HB of all this. We can have this document placed on the ELMO if Your Honours so wish. I have already distributed copies to the interpreters. However, based on this document, only on document Z733, the Trial Chamber concludes in paragraph 669 that Blaskic would not have undertaken these attacks without political approval, and the further conclusion is drawn that the top leadership was in fact the local leadership embodied in the person of Dario Kordic. They say that Blaskic could not easily have communicated with someone like Mate Boban in Mostar. This is the case that the Trial Chamber accepted. Based on this, the Chamber concluded that Kordic was linked with the issuing of orders to attack villages, including Rotilj. That's paragraph 669. I will repeat what my colleague Mr. Smith said. This refers -- this document refers only to the village of Gomionica, which is only one of ten villages in the Busovaca municipality. So I have to say I fail to see the link between this document and other villages, including Rotilj. The Chamber has reached similar conclusions with respect to events in 1993. Let me just remind you that the entire indictment and judgement was based on two events, or rather, two time periods, one in April and the other one in June. It was found that the villages of Tulica, Han Ploca and Grahovci, to the south of Kiseljak along the road to Sarajevo, were attacked on the 13th of June. The Trial Chamber considered, in accordance with what was said about the events in April, that these -- all these attacks were part of an unceasing attack by the HVO. The Trial Chamber accepted the statement of a witness about Kordic's presence in Kiseljak on the 14th of June, based on what the witness said that he had seen in passing in a five-second time period. I have to say that ever since we began working on this case long ago, in 1997, up to today, there has been a considerable development of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, and this is something that we are very pleased about, and it seems to us that this Tribunal's credibility is growing due to this. And this is also what my colleague Mr. Sayers mentioned about witness statements that have not been corroborated in any way. So both with respect to the attacks in June, based on this witness statement, the witness said that he had seen Mr. Kordic for five seconds, the attacks, according to the Trial Chamber, could not have been launched without the approval of the local political leadership in the person of Dario Kordic. Paragraph 726. And that is why Mr. Kordic was linked to the order that these attacks be launched. This, however, is what the evidence states. Kiseljak was a territory under the command of Ivica Rajic. Major Baggesen testified to this, transcript 7759. Brigadier Wingfield-Hayes, who testified two days before the close of the Prosecution case and who was the third in command in the UNPROFOR headquarters in Kiseljak, said that he had never seen Mr. Kordic in Kiseljak. Transcript 16168. And he also said that Mr. Kordic was not a person who should be consulted if there were any problems in Kiseljak, because Mr. Rajic was the local commander. I will not go into this any further. I will simply refer to the testimony of the Prosecution witness, Brigadier Winfield-Hayes. Let me say a few words about the location of these villages. Rotilj, as can be seen from the map adduced to the judgement, was located just to the rear, west of Kiseljak, in a valley above the town. Tulica, again, was militarily important because it was between the HVO and ABiH lines. Han Ploca/Grahovci, which are interconnected along the road, were militarily important because they were outside a main road junction, with key roads running to Sarajevo and Mostar. I am mentioning all this because I wish to say that the Trial Chamber failed to pay attention to this military aspect. All the villages I have mentioned, and some others as well, were in the area of war operations. Sometimes there were -- some of them were at the front line, others were being defended. For example, Witness AL, Prosecution witness, transcript 15554, said that the civilian population left Behrici, but 50 or 60 Muslim men stayed to fight and controlled the village for over two months. Behrici was part of the ABiH and the HVO front line. Prosecution Witness D says Gomionica was held by ABiH troops. Also Prosecution Witness AM, Major Baggesen, and others, made similar statements. The Trial Chamber, based on these two pieces of evidence, Z733 and Witness Y, considered that Mr. Kordic was linked to the events -- the attacks that took place in the Kiseljak municipality and that he was responsible, without mentioning any facts that would prove that Mr. Kordic participated in or planned any of these attacks, let alone proving elements of his mens rea. I do not want to waste time, so I think it is time to move on to slide 21, and this is what I wanted to point out. Z733, the Prosecution exhibit, deals only with the village of Gomionica, as explicitly stated in paragraph 1 of this document. In this order, Blaskic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In this order, Blaskic, among other things, in paragraph 4, on which the conclusion of the Trial Chamber is based, says: We have informed the very top of the HZ HB, with whom we are in constant communication, of all of this." The judgement says that the local politician, Mr. Kordic, embodies that top, but in the entire file, there is no document where Blaskic would use this expression "the very top." The very top, in this particular case, cannot refer to Mr. Kordic, because Mr. Kordic was not the very top of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. According to the way Colonel Blaskic addressed Mr. Kordic, this can mean only one thing. It can mean only the president of the community of Herceg-Bosna and his associates in Mostar, because, referring to Mr. Kordic, he always called him either "Mr. Kordic" or by his title, but never said about him that he was the very top. Mr. Kordic was not the very top, as the Trial Chamber itself concluded, saying that he was not in the highest echelons of power among the Bosnian Croats. Therefore, we contend that this is very stretched, this conclusion that Blaskic was referring to Kordic. What does this document show? It shows that Blaskic informed the very top of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, but it doesn't mean that he asked for approval from the very top of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to launch military action in the village of Gomionica only. We in the Defence fail to understand paragraph 769, that Blaskic would not have launched a military operation without the approval of Mr. Kordic. This is not a request for approval for an attack; it's only information as to what is happening in the village of Gomionica. In paragraph 839, we see what I said a moment ago, that the judgement itself considers that the evidence does not confirm that Kordic was -- that Kordic was at the top echelons of power in HB because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, we want to be very clear about the content of document 733. You were kind enough to give us a copy, and I don't know how best to do it. Unfortunately, it seems to be that the English translation does not correspond with the French translation. Therefore, if you could be so kind and read out the paragraphs you are referring to from this document and then it may help us. And I apologise to the interpreters to task you with translating something which is normally not your job.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have facilitated the work of the interpreters because I have prepared a copy for them. So they have the text in the three languages. I apologise that during the deliberations we didn't notice the errors in the translation, but the original, of course, is in Croatian, so I will read out point 1: "This evening you must take Gomionica or early in the morning." I think that is enough from that point 1, because no other place is mentioned and the operation is mentioned after that. And then we come to point 4 of this order, which says: "Generally, at all positions, the situation is under control. And we have informed the very top of the HZ HB of everything, with whom we are in constant contact." This point 4 is the reason for which Mr. Kordic, in my conviction, was convicted of everything and found guilty of everything done in Kiseljak in April 1993, because there was absolutely no other evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you, and the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, what my colleague said earlier on is this: It is one thing to establish a piece of evidence and then to see what the accused has done, which is simple, and then to ascertain the elements of his consciousness, the mens rea, and so on and so forth. Here, the Court, from a very pure and clear-cut document and clear-cut information about the events, comes to the conclusion in paragraph 669 that Blaskic would not have launched the attacks without political approval precisely of Mr. Kordic. Now, that is completely unacceptable to us and is a very weak argument, because it is not substantiated by proof and evidence. If we look at this document relating to Gomionica, which is a piece of information, and it draws conclusions for villages in the whole region, and then this information means political approval. I don't want to tire you with this point too much. I should like to go on to the next document, which is a very vital one as well. Everything that happened in June 1993 is based on the testimony of Witness Y, who testified on the 3rd and 4th of December, 1999. And the transcript is 11000 or thereabouts, some page or line thereabouts. Now, what did Witness Y actually say? Witness Y said that he saw Mr. Kordic at the barracks in Kiseljak and that at that point in time, Mr. Kordic was surrounded by some unknown individuals. He went on to say that he saw Mr. Kordic, as he was walking, while he was going to wash, and that he was 8 to 14 metres away from Mr. Kordic at that point in time, and both of them, as we have established, were moving, on the move, walking to and fro, and that all this lasted for a flat five seconds. So that is what the witness said. I do not wish to tire Your Honours or to repeat what my colleague Mr. Sayers has already said, but as I said a moment ago, with the development of jurisprudence in the Tribunal, which is progressing in the right direction, I would nonetheless like to say that this is something that has not been substantiated by any evidence and has not been substantiated by any witness testimony that Mr. Kordic was actually in Kiseljak. Mr. Kordic was a well-known personage. You would see him on television. Everybody knew what he looked like. And quite simply, in the judgement, mention is made of the fact that the Defence did not prove that Mr. Kordic was not in Kiseljak at the material time, that is to say, in June 1993. I fully accept the allegations made by Her Honour Judge Mumba that it is up to the Defence to prepare itself, to prepare the defence case, and to be trial-ready. However, I would like to say that it is almost impossible, or rather, absolutely impossible, to defend oneself from negative circumstances or to prove a negative circumstance at all. So therefore, it was impossible to prove that Mr. Kordic was not in Kiseljak from the 4th to the 8th or whatever the date was, as it says, in Kiseljak, because he was not able to be in Kiseljak in the first place. And even if he was in the barracks, this should have been -- rang the alarm bell for the Trial Chamber to focus on what the witness actually said, because in Kiseljak we had the centre of the UNPROFOR headquarters, Kiseljak was militarily interesting intelligence-wise. So they all oversaw the barracks. That is absolutely true, and nobody ever saw Mr. Kordic. And not a single document, all the milinfosums, not a single one of them, not a single intelligence report ever said that Mr. Kordic was ever seen in Kiseljak in the summer of 1993. And ultimately, Mr. Wingfield-Hayes didn't see him either, the number-three man in UNPROFOR. And I'm sure he would have heard -- had Mr. Kordic been there, and he was actually asked that in the courtroom. In a completely inexplicable way, the Trial Chamber accepted this gentleman's testimony that he had been -- that he had seen Mr. Kordic in some dramatic circumstances, according to him, and the Trial Chamber did not accept at least six or seven witness testimonies that Mr. Kordic was accused of. However -- and this was never corroborated. But let's move on. Let it be true that Witness Y did see Mr. Kordic, although we consider that that is impossible and that he must have made a mistake. Witness Y said nothing about what Mr. Kordic was doing; whether he was issuing any orders, whether he was committing any crimes, whether he was planning any crimes, ordering, planning any acts. All he did say was that he saw him passing by, passing by the corridor. I consider, and that is the position of my Defence, that -- and our Defence, that the Trial Chamber should have paid due attention to the testimony by Witness Y, especially as it based their stand on Mr. Kordic's participation in the crimes on that testimony and all the mens rea on the part of Kordic for those crimes. And the Trial Chamber failed to look into how Mr. Kordic could have been there in the first place. I think Witness O said something to that effect in the cross-examination during the trial, that Kiseljak was -- or rather, Busovaca was cut off from Kiseljak from the 24th of January, 1993, right up until the Washington Accords in the spring of 1994. So that is a fact. I do not wish to tire Your Honours now with some of the facts, for instance, the problem of identifying the individual. Mr. Sayers spoke about that at length. I would just like to indicate the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Vasiljevic trial judgement of the Trial Chamber, et cetera, and the Kupreskic judgement as well. Let me conclude. This document, Z733, in itself or with respect to any other evidence, does not show that Mr. Kordic should have given any political approval, neither did he have any part in the events that took place in the villages mentioned in April 1993. Also, on the basis of witness testimony, including the testimony of Witness Y, even if we do accept the conclusion made by the Trial Chamber that he did indeed see Mr. Kordic, all we can conclude from that is that Mr. Kordic was seen there, and nothing other than that, absolutely nothing. Let me remind you once again of the Krstic judgement with respect to the events in Potocari, because I think that that is the only reasonable solution in cases where there is not a shred of evidence to prove anything else other than that person was in one place at one time. Otherwise, if any of us happens to be just by chance -- and I apologise for this comparison, but if it so happens that we happened to be somewhere where somebody was killed, we would all be murderers or be incriminated. So looking -- and this is quite unacceptable from the legal aspect and from the aspects of life in general. So this is not sufficient to prove guilt. And I put it to you that there is no proof and evidence that Mr. Kordic had any power or influence to wield influence of the events in Kiseljak. The attacks there, as I have said, in view of military targets, were justified, and it has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt that the operations were illegal and unlawful, that they were attacks against civilians, or rather, civilian facilities, and there is no proof of this, that it was military necessity either. And it is for all these reasons, as far as this part of my presentation is concerned, that the only reasonable conclusion is that Mr. Kordic -- that nothing was proved that Mr. Kordic had any connection at all with these events, least of all that these two pieces of evidence, document 733 and Witness Y testimony, would be sufficient to establish his guilt. I have overstepped my time somewhat. I did want to make certain other points about the events in the village of Loncari and Donja Veceriska and Gacice, however, I will now cede the floor to Mr. Sayers and we'll see whether we'll go into those points later on if there's time. Thank you. I apologise. Of course, if there are any questions from Your Honours, I should be happy to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Guney, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, I must say that I'm a little perplexed, faced with the terms that were used by you and by your colleagues during your submissions, with respect to the prerogatives and power and authority of Mr. Kordic. Now, would you try and assist us, please, and help us clarify certain points. Because on the one hand, he was a man of politics, he was a civilian exerting considerable influence and power in Central Bosnia, on the one hand, according to paragraphs 836 of the judgement, for example, and 839, although he played an important role in military affairs and sometimes even going towards giving orders and controlling HVO forces. "While he played an important role in military matters," et cetera, et cetera, paragraph 839. Finally, we come to document Z733 and the fourth paragraph, in which it says that the situation is under control at all the positions and we have informed the top leadership of everything and we are in constant contact with the leadership. I think that you said that they exerted influence. Sometimes you used the word "authority," exerted authority. Your colleague used similar terms. So I think we should spend some time to actually delve into what we mean by this authority. What was the authority, influence, and prerogatives of Mr. Kordic, in actual fact, in light of the elements that I have just quoted? So would you be so kind as to help us out on this point, please, and develop arguments to help us clarify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I shall be happy to do so, Judge Guney. May I just make a few statements before that? The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, as my colleague said before me, had its civilian structures of authority and the military chain of command. Mr. Kordic was a politician who did not have any administrative authority in Central Bosnia, because the Prime Minister of the civilian government of the HVO, Mr. Brnik, had his deputy. He was Ante Valenta, and he had his headquarters in that same Lasva River Valley. Therefore, all these civilian organs of power and authority in the municipalities of Busovaca, Vitez, and Novi Travnik were, in actual fact, subordinated - I'm talking about civilian authorities - to Mr. Valenta, as the "deputy of the Prime Minister" of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And from this, we come to what I want to tell you: Mr. Kordic was a politician. He did not have any administrative authorisations and competences or military ones either. He started his political career, if I can put it that way, within the party to which he belonged, and he belonged to the party since the beginning of 1990 or 1991. Later on, he grew to become, and of course circumstances pushed him in that direction, he became a sort of popular tribune in the Lasva River valley, and that in fact is reflected in the judgement in paragraph 839, that he remained a civilian. So he remained a civilian with no administrative powers. He couldn't, for instance, replace the president of the civilian HVO in the Busovaca municipality, Mr. Maric. He didn't have the authority to do that, for example. Therefore, he was a politician who emanated from the party and became a popular Tribune with great authority among the people. People came to him for assistance, asked for his help, and that is how Mr. Kordic came to be involved in some circumstances and events. The Convoy of Joy, for example, in the summer of June 1993, not far from Vitez, where Mr. Kordic, by wielding his authority, endeavoured to have certain problems resolved. So people came to him for help. He was an individual without any administrative authority or competencies. That's who Mr. Kordic was. So when I and my colleagues speak about certain authority and influence, we mean political influence that he wielded, not actual power in his hands to undertake one thing or another thing in the administrative or military sense at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I just have a follow-up question. I'm aware that you dealt with Kiseljak and the surrounding municipalities. However, let's please have a look on paragraph 577 of the judgement. And please accept this as a question under the heading "Right to be heard." Isn't it true that it seems to be that there Mr. Blaskic and Mr. Kordic acted apparently on the same level, if not -- it's referred to -- if this tape is not disputed, and the intercept, Kordic saying to Mr. Blaskic: 100 should be killed for every one friend. There was a close link between the politicians and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't hear what he said. What was the quote?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I quoted from the intercept of January 1993. You can find it in paragraph 577 of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have seen that. Mr. President, the situation, as far as the Defence is concerned, is quite simple in this regard. The question and the date, and Mr. Smith said a moment ago, who attacked whom in January 1993. Therefore, the strong forces of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, who were preparing, as has been proved, were on the attack. And of course, the position of the people who were within the pocket was to do anything they could. Now, what Mr. Kordic and Blaskic spoke about, their conversation, and he was the other side of the pocket in Kiseljak, he went to visit his father, as far as I gather, is essentially - I don't know how else I can say this, and I think we said this once in our response - was a joke, an unrealistic fact. This never actually happened. This event never actually happened. There was no VBR that was attacking, nor were there any consequences of that. And so the tone of the entire conversation is one of joking. And we can see that it is not a conversation between people planning to launch a serious military attack. And that is what we claimed all along, and the tape proved that in itself. So there were no consequences, nor did this event ever take place, this shelling, I mean. It never took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Weinberg de Roca, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a follow-up question following Judge Guney's question. It's difficult to understand -- you and your colleagues are speaking about administrative authority or influence, political authority or influence, and military authority or influence. And it's the submission, I understand, or I understand, at least, that Mr. Kordic had political but not administrative or military authority. Did this political authority mean that he had authority over the paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not, madam, Your Honour. It is true that we state that Mr. Kordic did not have administrative authority, but we also claim that he didn't have any military authority, and numerous witnesses have borne that out. Now, this might appear to be a little illogical, but in our defence case we heard testimony from the main people and assistants of General Blaskic, from his first deputy, the chief of staff, several commanders in his brigade, brigades under Mr. Blaskic. So it is crystal clear that Mr. Kordic did not have any military authority. And similarly, no power at all - perhaps power would be a good word in English - over any paramilitaries, paramilitary formations. Now, the difference and distinction between political and administrative authority is very vital. Let me quote an example. In Busovaca there was no food, for example. That was a case in point. The local authorities in Busovaca had their own mechanisms of how to deal with the situation, how to collect food. And when they were not able to have food supplies from normal sources, if I can use that term, or from UNPROFOR, then they went to prevail upon Mr. Kordic, to ask him, as a man they could believe, to wield his authority and go and see with UNPROFOR, to send a telegram to Mostar, or however else, so that the food could be found. And Mr. Kordic would solve the problem and the food supplies would arrive in a few days' time, and the people were exhilarated, but of course he wasn't able to order anyone to do this. So that's what I mean, that's how he was a general type politician, if I can put it that way. He had no administrative or civilian authority or military authority, let alone exert an influence on any paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No more questions. And it would be once again for Mr. Sayers, but I think it's fair enough. You are prepared for another half an hour and then I think we should continue now for the first 15 minutes, up to 5.00, and then you may continue for another 15 minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might just follow up on the question that was asked by Judge Weinberg de Roca with some specific references to the actual testimony. Let me first point the Appeals Chamber's attention to the slide that we've put on. This is the UNPROFOR -- sorry. This is General Blaskic's chief of staff, Brigadier Franjo Nakic, who testified quite unequivocally at trial that Mr. Kordic had no military role. Next. Brigadier Darko Gelic was the UNPROFOR liaison officer. He was asked, actually, the precise question that Judge Weinberg de Roca asked: "Did Mr. Kordic have any military authority over any units of the military police or any special purpose units, paramilitary units?" "No." "Did you ever see Mr. Kordic give orders to Colonel Blaskic?" "No." "Did you ever hear that Mr. Kordic ever tried to give orders to Mr. Blaskic or influence his military decisions in any way?" "No." "Did he have any authority over the Jokers, the Vitezovi, the 4th Battalion of the military police?" "No." But who better to know whether there was authority over the military police than the commander of the military police? Let's see what he had to say. He was called as a Court witness. Colonel Marinko Palavra, the successor to Ljubicic. He testified he was subordinate to the operative zone and to the command of the operative zone. "Is that correct?" "It is." "Did you ever take orders, directions or instructions from Dario Kordic ever?" "Your Honours, no, never." TR27014. "Did Kordic ever try to exert military influence over the soldiers under your -- military police under your command or the soldiers under Colonel Blaskic's command to your knowledge?" "He absolutely never did." "As far as you're aware, Kordic had no authority whatsoever over the military police?" He agreed with that. The proposition was put to him that "You took your orders from your superior commander who, on August 1st, was Colonel Blaskic; is that so?" "That is quite so." Kordic had nothing to do with the running of the units, including the military police. And if I may go into private session for just one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Your Honours, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to clean that up, since there was some lack of clarity in the record on that. I'd like to make three points as we draw to the close here. We've got our heads down and we're headed for the finish line, I hope. Armed conflict, international armed conflict, and sentencing. Armed conflict. There was no armed conflict before April of 1993. And how do we know that? Because the Trial Chamber told us that. We know that this is very important in the Tribunal's jurisprudence because the armed conflict requirement is a jurisdictional requirement for the application -- for the finding of any crimes under Articles 3 or 5. Or Article 2, for that matter, but there must be an international armed conflict under 2. What does it mean? It means armed force between states, which we don't have here, or protracted armed violence. The key factual finding by the Trial Chamber here is paragraph 31 of the judgement. It was not until April 1993 that a generalised state of armed conflict in the form of protracted violence broke out in the territory of Central Bosnia between the HVO and the ABiH. The Trial Chamber then confusingly and incorrectly, we would submit to the Appeals Chamber, said before that there were only localised areas of conflict. Within which, it said, a state of armed conflict could be said to occur. But that's not possible. To be a state of armed conflict it has to be protracted, and as paragraph 31 of the judgement recognises, protracted armed violence did not break out anywhere in Central Bosnia until April of 1993. I won't belabour the definition of protracted. We've put various dictionary definitions up on the screen for you. But Kordic respectfully submits that by no stretch of the imagination could the brief flare-up of fighting in Novi Travnik be referred to as protracted armed violence. What was it? We know what it was. The Prosecution itself has made the submission that the 16th of April, 1993 attacks by the HVO were entirely different to what had occurred prior to that date. To use -- and the Prosecution cited the very graphic and accurate testimony of one of the BritBat military witnesses, the subordinate of Lieutenant Colonel Stewart, Major Watters, who actually described what had occurred before the protracted armed violence broke out in April 1993 as "local punch-ups between small communities in different villages." And that's exactly what we had in Novi Travnik and in Busovaca in January 1993, punch-ups between small communities, skirmishes. There was no jurisdiction over them. And the Naletilic trial judgement has reached virtually the same conclusion that we're urging to the Appeals Chamber today, and that was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. although tensions gradually increased between the HVO and the ABiH in Mostar, not in Central Bosnia, it only turned into a full-scale conflict in mid-April 1993, and the Naletilic Trial Chamber specifically ruled that armed conflict existed since 17th of April, 1993 in the relevant area. If I may turn to international armed conflict. Our submissions on this are very particular and very narrow. First, the legal consequences of the characterisation of a conflict are particularly important, as the Tadic appeals judgement said. Article 2 of the Statute applies only when an international armed conflict exists. Which counts are affected in this case? Count 8, count 12, and count 22, we would submit. Now, what was the governing test of how to determine what an armed conflict was before the 15th of January, 1999? We know that. It was the International Court of Justice leading case of Nicaragua from the 27th of June, 1986. What did that require? A high degree of control. And even when the state allegedly, internationalising a conflict, had participated in the financing, organisation, training, logistical matters, even when the international influence resulted in the selection of military or paramilitary targets by the state, even when the state participated in planning the operations of the paramilitary units, even if that was preponderant or decisive, that is still not enough to internationalise the conflict according to the jurisprudence established by the Nicaragua case. Without the foreign entity exercising effective control over the troops, there was no international armed conflict. That was the law that existed as of 1986. This test was changed on the 15th of July, 1999, in the Tadic appeals judgement where this Chamber held that, with respect, it held the Nicaragua test not to be persuasive. Having found that that test was not consonant with the law of state responsibility or with judicial or state practice, the Appeals Chamber departed from it, and that's exactly what the Naletilic trial judgement accurately observed. Instead, a new test was established; overall control. What's the difference? Well, the difference is that this is a much lower test. The requirement of overall control is nowhere near as rigorous as the requirement of effective control. And the Aleksovski appeals judgement paragraph 145 specifically ruled that and stated that the overall control test was a new, lower test. Under the principle of nullum crimen sine lege, an offence will only fall within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal if that offence was recognised as a form of liability under customary international law as it existed at the time the offence was committed, which here was 1992 or 1993, when the Nicaragua test was still in effect, six years before this Chamber changed the governing law in the Tadic Appeals Chamber. I might also say that the defective indictment in this case fails to allege the identity of the entity assertedly exercising overall control over HVO forces in Central Bosnia. As a result, similar omissions resulted in the Simic trial judgement, the Trial Chamber rejecting any consideration of the allegedly international nature of the conflict because the indictment had not alleged the specific identity of the foreign entity assertedly exercising overall control. The same result in Hadzihasanovic -- not the same result but a similar result, because the Prosecution was required to allege the indictment in that case to assert the identity of the entity assertedly exercising overall control. So our conclusion on this point is very, very simple: There was a new standard, a lower standard articulated on the 15th of July, 1999. It governs conduct after that date, no question about it, but not before. And to conclude otherwise would violate the principle of legality. And with the Appeals Chamber's permission, the Appeals Chamber wants to take the break now, I'll conclude my comments very shortly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I hope to conclude in about 15 minutes with the sentencing appeal arguments made by Mr. Kordic. And the reason that that is so is because there are two things in Article 24(2) of the Tribunal's Statute that must be taken into account. Obviously the Trial Chamber has to take into account the gravity of the offence, but also the Trial Chamber is equally obliged to take into account the individual circumstances of the convicted person. Obviously if the Trial Chamber failed to take into account the gravity of the offence, then it would arguably have committed an error of law. The same is true if it fails to take into account the family -- the individual circumstances of the accused person. This is an error of law. The individual circumstances of Mr. Kordic were not really controverted at trial. He was the oldest of five children. His father is a retired veterinarian. His mother is a retired paediatrician. Thank you. The law on this issue is relatively simple. The Appeals Chamber noted in that case that it is not clear why the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. President. If I may begin, Your Honours. It's the Prosecution's position that the judgement in this case starts at the beginning in May of 1992, and there's ample evidence to show the role that the appellant played from May of 1992 right through until the end of the time period for which he was convicted. The briefs are quite full, as I'm sure you're aware, so I'll try and deal with the issues that were just dealt with today or address the ones that I can try and assist the Court on. First of all, the general allegation made at the beginning - or submission, I'm sorry - by my learned friend was that access was denied to all the closed-session material and that it was because of the Prosecution's guarantee, for Rule 68 purpose, that he was denied.
