utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. The second point I wanted to make about the closed session is that throughout the brief, and to a certain extent throughout the submissions, the focus is always on the Prosecution's failure to provide the evidence or on the Prosecution's failure to ensure access to closed session. Please keep in mind that the law at the time regarding access to closed session was very different than the law that applies now, and the obligation is on my learned friend to point out the error by the Trial Chamber. And as an Appellate Court, you're fully aware that that's the ultimate goal here, is to determine whether the Trial Chamber erred and what the impact of that error is. Regarding the disclosure of Witness AT, the appellant said that he was disclosed just at the end of trial and he testified one week before the end of trial. Once again, the insinuation was that there was some attempt by the Prosecution or some action by the Prosecution which resulted in a violation of some disclosure obligation. I simply ask you to take note of the Trial Chamber's ruling on this. The Trial Chamber decided, on September the 26th, 2000, that in fact, and I'm -- well, I'll refer -- it's in closed session, so I'm not going into closed session. I'll simply ask you to look at the Trial Chamber's decision on the motion to call Witness AT on the 26th of September, 2000, in which the explanation that was provided by the Prosecution as to when the decision was made and why the decision was made to call Witness AT, that was completely accepted by the Trial Chamber, with no objection at the time by counsel for Kordic. To come now and say that somehow there was some disclosure violation when there was no allegation at the time the Court gave the explanation. Further, the Court decided at the time that it would put off the hearing of Witness AT until the end of the case so that they had two months in which to prepare their submissions. And in fact, I'd ask you to take note of the Trial Chamber's comments on the 26th of September, in which they point out that counsel for Mr. Kordic frankly and properly conceded on behalf of Mr. Kordic that he cannot object to the Prosecution calling this witness and that he submits that the evidence should be called in rebuttal. The Trial Chamber agreed and added that this would be an advantage of curing any alleged unfairness. Once again, I'd ask that the Court please keep in mind the decisions of the Trial Chamber when dealing with these allegations. Those were the two aspects of the disclosure, belated disclosure, that was mentioned today. The rest are dealt with in the brief. If I can now turn to the Rule 68 allegation. As this Court is fully aware, in the Krstic decision, there's two steps. The first is that there must be a demonstration of a violation, and the second is that there must be material prejudice that was suffered. The Court in the Krstic case and the Appeals Chamber in the Akayesu case has held that the remedy is one that can -- if there is a violation, the remedy is to try and put the evidence that was not admitted, or excluded, in fact, by the allegation of Prosecution violation, to bring that through admission of additional evidence in the Court. That's quite clear. It's in the Krstic decision. And in the Krstic decision, the Defence was able to take advantage of that. And despite the fact that they both at the same time made a Rule 68 allegation and a 115 allegation, the material was at least before the Court so it could properly assess whether the evidence was exculpatory. I point out as a matter of procedure that you do not have the Blaskic material before you. I quite frankly don't know how you're going to assess whether it's exculpatory and I don't know how you're going to assess it in light of the total nature of the testimony, all of the testimony, to determine whether or not the passages relied upon by my learned friend are accurate and whether they're clarified at any point in time throughout the testimony. That was the Prosecution's submission in the filing, that these allegations cannot be made in a vacuum. And I'm not talking about the filing of the material as 115 evidence. That's clearly not been done. In fact, my learned friend, when asked by the Pre-Appeal Judge whether he wanted to rely on it and file any additional material, said that he was not. If you recall the filing that Mr. Kordic did immediately after Mr. Cerkez filed his 115 motion, you will recall that Mr. Kordic took a somewhat different position on the additional evidence than Mr. Cerkez. In fact, he opposed some of Mr. Cerkez's additional evidence. But in one of his filings, he indicated that he reserved the right to submit evidence, and particularly the closed-session testimony of Colonel Blaskic at the time, if that evidence was such that it was crucial to the case and if it could affect the verdict. In fairness to the Defence, they relied on the wording of Rule 115. Once they got the closed-session testimony of Colonel Blaskic - and it's fair; they got it in the appellate proceedings. We provide it to them - they did not attempt to submit that evidence before you. And in fact, they didn't attempt to put it before you for the purposes of the Rule 68 allegation. And in my respectful submission, without putting that material before you, you're in no position to decide whether or not that evidence actually constitutes Rule 68. Secondly, as we've said in our filing, the Defence has to put that forward at least, in our submission, on a prima facie basis that it's truthful. In other words, this is evidence they would put to a witness for the purpose of cross-examination or this is evidence that they would call themselves. There's something, with respect, something irrational about the approach. If this is such crucial evidence that is so clearly, on its face, exculpatory, and is so obviously exculpatory that would demonstrate that Mr. Kordic has no control in Central Bosnia, why wasn't it filed? If this evidence is so crucial that witnesses would have been cross-examined differently, it's respectfully submitted that the failure to seek to admit it, at least to file it with the Court, or to demonstrate quite clearly what witnesses would have been cross-examined differently and how that could have affected the verdict, without that showing, in my respectful submission, though the Court may render a decision on the scope of Rule 68, there is no basis for a remedy, as there's clearly no material prejudice. And I note that in relation to both the testimony of -- the testimony that was referred to today, and I'll leave it to the submissions of today, which was the Blaskic testimony. The appellant referred to two of the Prosecution's submissions in relation to the testimony. The first was the Prosecution's submission in the Blaskic appeal that the Prosecution put forward Blaskic's testimony that Kordic was not in the military chain of command. Just to make it clear -- and I think I appreciate my friend's position that this demonstrates that the Prosecution knew about this testimony at the time and should have disclosed it. I think that's his position. But in his brief, he also puts it forward as if it's the Prosecution's position as to the truth of the contents of the testimony. I just want to make it clear that the Prosecution does not take the position that Blaskic's testimony is the truth. It does not take the position that Blaskic's claims that Kordic was not involved and had no role in the military operations is the true state of affairs. And it was put forward in the Prosecution's submissions to show that Colonel Blaskic has specifically changed his position on appeal, at least to the extent that his filings and his submissions and his additional evidence has changed his position on appeal, in light of the fact that he never testified to that. I note that if this evidence was to be admitted as additional evidence, if there was an application, it would have been the Prosecution's position, as we've set out, that he should be called as a witness and he should testify as to the propositions for which the Defence is alleging his evidence stands for. In the Kupreskic appeal, there was a paragraph put forward with respect to the Prosecution's submissions regarding AT's knowledge or his awareness of the nature and content of the political meeting. Those submissions were made in the context of the knowledge of Vlatko Kupreskic and whether Vlatko Kupreskic was in the chain of command, the political or the military hierarchy, and that in the preceding paragraph there's a discussion about how there were political and military hierarchical structures where information, orders, and assignments were handed out, and that the point was that obviously Witness AT, who was not at the meeting, would not be in a position and would not be privy to the specific nature and contents of that political meeting. But that doesn't preclude the Kordic Trial Chamber or this Court from accepting the inference that the political meeting authorised the orders that came out of the military meeting. I'd next like to deal with the submissions that the violation was deliberate. It may just be the nature of the allegation, I think - and I stand to be corrected, of course, by my learned friend - that when the use of the term "deliberate" was made in the submissions, it was made in the sense that there was a conscious decision not to disclose Blaskic's closed-session testimony, and that is the position. It's not that there was a deliberate and intentional decision to withhold evidence which the Prosecution knew to be exculpatory. There is a difference, and I want to make it clear that it was deliberately withheld because there was a view that it wasn't exculpatory, not that the Prosecution was acting in bad faith and deliberately intending to withhold it in the hopes of obtaining a conviction. The Prosecution at trial was of the view that this could not constitute Rule 68 evidence, in light of the number of factors which are set out in the annex to the Prosecution's filing and in relation to -- and set out in the Prosecution's submissions. The issue for this Court, in my respectful submission, is not to -- well, it is to actually assess and decide on the issue of credibility. To what extent can credibility affect the obligation of the Prosecution under Rule 68? Is there ever a circumstance where the evidence is so unbelievable or, to accept the standard under Rule 115, not reasonably capable of belief that it would not be unacceptable for the Prosecution to not disclose it? I think it's fair to say that in the majority of cases, credibility is a matter to be left for the Bench. It's a matter to be left for the Judges, and whether the Prosecution generally thinks it's credible or not, that's a matter for the Bench if the evidence is called. But the issue in this case is whether in the circumstances, as set out in the Prosecution's brief, it was unreasonable in these circumstances to consider that that was a factor in the determination of Rule 68. It also must be remembered it was a number of years ago these assessments were being made. The law has developed, and quite rightly, in this area, but at the time it was being developed there was some uncertainty. There were very few decisions with respect to Rule 68 at the time. It doesn't necessarily justify it if it was -- if it should have been disclosed, but it does demonstrate that there was -- there wasn't some clear guidance at that time. And it was also at a time where there were many people working on it and different approaches from different systems. I'm not particularly familiar with the civil law system, but an accused or a co-accused is, as I understand it, not considered a witness in relation to a civil law system, so the approach at the time was maybe somewhat unclear. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. But the Rule, Rule 68, does indicate that the language says evidence or information. So to that extent, if that's the Court -- and if the Court may well decide that credibility is not a factor for the Prosecution to take into consideration, then we'll accept that the -- the decision is that it should have been disclosed. There were two other aspects in relation to this deliberate allegation. I think I've characterised my learned friend's position correctly, and I've certainly tried to make clear our understanding of what the position is in relation to the deliberate nature or the conscious and intentional decision not to disclose because the Prosecution didn't consider it to fall under Rule 68, but there were two other examples. One was referred to today. It was in relation to Witness AO, and it was referred to by my learned friend in his submissions on a violation in relation to Rule 68. I simply ask that you note the Prosecution's submission in its brief and the comments made by the senior trial attorney in the transcripts. They're in private session, so I won't go into them, I'll just inform you of them. At page 27143 of the -- of the transcripts wherein the Prosecution sets out the fact that it was the Prosecution, after Witness AO had testified, that actually asked that further searches be done in relation to this witness, and then when those further searches brought up additional information, it was disclosed to the Defence immediately afterwards, and then the Court ruled on the issue and actually excluded the testimony of Witness AO because Witness AO declined to come back for further cross-examination after the evidence had been given to the Defence and they sought to cross-examine him. In my respectful submission, this actually demonstrates compliance by the Prosecution, diligent efforts, and the fact that the Trial Chamber took specific steps to ensure there was no prejudice. The last example I would like to refer you to is an example referred to in passing in the appellant's brief. It relates to a witness named EE. For those of you familiar with the Kupreskic case, Witness EE was a witness in the Kupreskic case, a victim, and who testified in closed session, so at one point in time I will have to go into private session so as not to reveal the contents of a discussion that took place during the Kordic trial. Witness EE was the witness who testified about the participation of AT in the attack on Ahmici, and Witness EE was evidence that the Defence asked for for the purpose of cross-examining Witness AT. In the Defence's view, they thought that this evidence could be used to discredit Witness AT when he testified by asking him about the evidence that was accepted by the Kupreskic Trial Chamber. On October 13, 2000 - this is after the Court had ordered that Witness AT be called but still six weeks before he was called - the Trial Chamber ruled that they could not disclose Witness EE's testimony to the Defence. Though Witness EE's testimony would clearly be relevant to the testimony of AT, the Trial Chamber said that it could not disclose it because Witness EE had refused to agree and provide consent to the disclosure of the testimony. So the Trial Chamber denied the motion for access to Witness EE's testimony and told the Defence that they would have to proceed with the cross-examination of AT without it. Now, I'd like to just go into private session, if I may, at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I simply wanted to make this point to make it clear that when you're looking at the obligations of the Prosecution and the disclosure in this case, that this exhibits the fair and professional conduct of the Prosecution to guarantee the fairness of the trial. And this also was in relation to Witness AT, the witness who the Prosecution called in relation to the meeting, as you know, in which the Prosecution took steps to ensure that the Defence had ample material by which to cross-examine. If I may, I'll move on to the indictment issues. Once again, in my respectful submission, the starting point is first of all whether or not there was a complaint at trial on the indictment; and secondly, if there was a decision as a result of that complaint, whether that decision was in error. That's the starting point and my submission for this Chamber. Despite the submissions by my learned colleagues, they have not attempted to demonstrate that the Trial Chamber was wrong in its ultimate decision to not have the amended indictment provide further particulars, and that decision arose out of a hearing on the 16th of February, 1999. And I won't read you, but I'll paraphrase that what Judge May said was that the Defence arguments do have or may have more force the closer you get to trial, and that the Prosecution should consider including in the pre-trial brief securing the various counts and tying them to the allegations. Counsel for the Defence, Mr. Geneson indicates -- he indicates to the Court that he appreciates that the Trial Chamber has indicated an interest and a direction to the Prosecution to resolve some of these vagueness issues, and then says: "We appreciate that." He does state that until the pre-trial brief is filed, they're still handicapped because of the fact that they still are basing the preparation of their case on the indictment and not the pre-trial brief, but he says that handicap remains until the pre-trial brief is filed. There was no subsequent motion after receipt of the pre-trial brief for further particulars, as far as I am aware. To deal with the notice of the mode of liability, I think it was Mr. -- I may be wrong. I'm not sure if there was Mr. Sayers or Mr. Smith, but one of my learned colleagues indicated that -- raised the issue whether the mode of liability itself -- there was notice of the mode of liability, that being common criminal plan. There is language throughout the indictment which comments on the fact that Mr. Kordic was acting with others and he was acting with others in both the political, military campaign, but also in relation to the underlying counts in the indictment. He refers to paragraph 26 of the indictment and notes that though this may contain some inkling of the third form of joint criminal enterprise, it's insufficient. In my respectful submission, it's actually quite remarkable that, at a time when the Tadic Appeals Chamber had not come out and where there had not been a determination of the exact wording needed for notice, that the Prosecution, in fact, uses the words "acting together" and "acting jointly," and in paragraph 26, speaks about the acts of Mr. Kordic and the fact that "he was aware of and had every reason to know of the dangers, abuses, and consequences of the campaign's policies and objectives and the courses of conduct that he and others set in motion." It then goes on and lists the actions that would follow and says that they were fully foreseeable. In my respectful submission, that's fairly close in terms of JCE 3, when there wasn't a particular formulation of wording of the JCE that could be included in the indictment. In my respectful submission, the early decisions of Tadic and others that talk about acting together are clear support for that form of liability. But when the pre-trial brief was disclosed on March 25th, it's much more extensive in terms of providing notice of the mode of liability. I'd ask you to look through paragraphs 24. I won't take you through the pre-trial brief, but paragraph 24, paragraph 118, paragraph 119, and paragraph 120. In my submission, those paragraphs of the pre-trial brief clearly put the accused on notice that the mode of liability has been charged. And in fact, in paragraph 119, the Furundzija judgement is quoted in the pre-trial brief, commenting on the recognition of the notion of common design and joint criminal enterprise. It further states that "is a knowing participant in a common plan or design," and that, therefore, "liability is incurred for all acts that flow from a plan, irrespective of whether he was involved in the act." They cite from the Celebici Trial Chamber judgement, where it refers to common plan or design where members of a group are acting with common criminal purpose. It's clear that the pre-trial brief, combined with the indictment, charged common criminal plan and joint criminal enterprise. It's interesting that in the Defence pre-trial brief -- in this case, the Defence opted to file a pre-trial brief before the trial started, as was their right, and they filed a pre-trial brief about a week before the trial started. And in the Defence brief before the trial starts, they have legal submissions on the forms of co-perpetration, the forms of co-principles, what constitutes indirect responsibility, and challenges the common criminal plan, or this form is vicarious liability. It's quite clear before the trial started that everyone was operating from the same basis. There was a comment by one of my learned friends about the lack of notice of victims. There is also an acknowledgement of the sheer scale of this case. To list all the victims would be essentially to list most of the witnesses, which you find in annex 3, I think it is, to the pre-trial brief. Annex 3 to the pre-trial brief sets out a page of material which lists the accused, the count, the location, the dates, and then every single location and every witness that will testify on that location. Now, it doesn't specify it, quite frankly, as victims, but it's quite clear when you look at them that a number of these are victims of the crimes that took place. There is the question of notice of the membership in a JCE specific to the appellant, and the indictment speaks about the Bosnian Croat leadership and lists them as members of the HDZ, the Herceg-Bosna community and the HVO. There's no doubt that the HVO included Colonel Blaskic at the time. You will recall that there was actually an original indictment, and in that original indictment Colonel Blaskic was severed because he was already in the Tribunal's custody and started his trial before Mr. Kordic arrived, and if you look at the original indictment, which is on the record, it charges Blaskic and Kordic jointly with the unlawful attacks. It charges Kordic and Blaskic with planning and executing a systematic campaign. It charges Blaskic, Kordic, and Cerkez in the unlawful attacks and destruction in Vitez municipality conducted by HVO forces under Cerkez. It talks about HVO forces under the direction of Kordic and Blaskic arresting and detaining, some of them through the Vitez Brigade and Mario Cerkez. In the pre-trial brief it lists that the members of the group include the leading members of the Presidency. That's paragraph 65 of the pre-trial brief. In the Defence pre-trial brief filed on April 6th, there is a discussion as to an explanation of the Herceg-Bosna community and its membership. There's also a discussion about the distribution of power between the president, the vice-president, the HVO and their relationship. There is an organisational scheme of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna after the establishment of the HVO, and there's a report by the president, Mate Boban, of Herceg-Bosna, regarding Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1991 to 1993. In my submission, there can be no doubt that Mr. Kordic knew who the senior members and Bosnian Croat leaders were in Herceg-Bosna, in the HDZ, and in the HVO. And lastly, you may not be aware of this, but when the original indictment was filed, there was the original indictment, the supporting material, and a statement of facts. There actually was a 40-page statement of facts attached to the original indictment which was then refiled on March the 9th by the Prosecution with one of its filings and incorporated in its pre-trial brief. So you essentially have two pre-trial briefs, the one on March 25th and the one on March 9th which the Defence got with the original supporting material. That statement of fact sets out the key members of the -- sets out that the key members are who were involved, including Kordic and Blaskic. It sets out the Herceg-Bosna -- members of the Herceg-Bosna Presidency - Kordic, Valenta and Kostroman - it sets out the role of Kordic as he is charged jointly with Blaskic, and it sets out Mr. Kordic's de facto and de jure control. Without going through all the specifics to his -- sorry, the allegations putting him on notice of his participation in the JCE, there is the original indictment which sets out the specific role in paragraphs 9, 10, 24, and 40. There's a listing of the actions by which he participated in paragraph 10, which includes negotiating cease-fires, issuing orders of a military nature, authorising travel and movement, negotiating the passage of convoys. Then there's the original indictment which the Defence got which actually specifies the planning, execution, or direction of Kordic and Blaskic. Then there's the statement of facts. Without going through them all, I'd ask you, if it will assist the Court, that in the statement of facts which they received with the original material and which was incorporated as part of the record, it lists in paragraph 8 the key members of Herceg-Bosna, including Kordic and Blaskic. It lists the other members who were charged in the indictment; Kordic, Blaskic, Cerkez, Santic, Skopljak, and Aleksovski. It lists a number of paragraphs of the de facto power and gives examples of Kordic's ability to exercise that de facto power. Interestingly, it includes the October 1992 incident in Novi Travnik. It lists a number of times that Blaskic gives orders. It lists the time when Blaskic negotiated the release of three detained Muslim girls. Has three or four allegations regarding April, and it lists Blaskic's participation in the Convoy of Joy in June 1993 when the soldiers present would not release the convoy without orders from Kordic. And lastly, in the pre-trial brief, the Prosecution attached annex 1, and annex 1 is a chronology of every single day, date, location, event, fact or event, and source, and it lists the -- all the evidence of the participation of Kordic and Cerkez. This annex is the annex of the evidence relating to their participation. I think it's somewhere in the region of 56 pages long and somewhere in the range of 600 entries. In my respectful submission, there was ample evidence putting the appellant on notice, either in the indictment itself or, as recognised by the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber, through the other means by which notice can be provided. I just wanted to make a few submissions on the allegation that the case was a moving target for the Defence. First of all, they allege that the meeting on April the 15th is a material fact, material fact in the sense that it would be something that should have been listed in the indictment. The Prosecution's submission, without going through all the material I have prepared, is that the -- a meeting is not a material fact. What the indictment must do for a material fact is set out the role and participation to put him on notice. There were other meetings that took place. There was the meeting in Novi Travnik when he and Blaskic issued the order leading military operations. There was a meeting with Colonel Duncan where civilians would not move except for on the express orders of Kordic. There was a meeting, or at least a communication, in Kiseljak where Blaskic reports that he had informed the leadership of the HZ HB of the actions taking place in Kiseljak. I could probably list about 10 or 15 examples where the Court found certain meetings to take place, meetings of the direct involvement and participation of Mr. Kordic, and many of them referred to and accepted by the Trial Chamber subsequently in its judgement. It's respectfully submitted that every meeting that took place that involved his direct participation in some sort of either military or political action that resulted in the -- well, the allegations put forward by the Prosecution in the indictment, the indictment would essentially become the pre-trial brief. I'd also note that when Witness AT was called, when there was a motion to bring Witness AT on September 25th, the Defence for Mr. Cerkez actually raised the fact that this was a material fact. During the submission, counsel for Cerkez said: This evidence by Witness AT about this meeting, it's a material fact and should have been in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY DISAGREED AND SAID
utterances.text: No, this is a matter of evidence. At that hearing on the 25th, when the Defence made their submissions, counsel for Kordic did not join in the submissions of counsel for Cerkez. Counsel for Kordic did not take the position that it was a material fact. In its subsequent written opposition to the Prosecution's rebuttal evidence, they did not take the position that it was a material fact which required it to be in the indictment. The appellant has indicated in his submission that the evidence of Witness AT represents a change in the Prosecution case from 7(3) to a 7(1), a shift from vicarious liability to an involvement in the direct operations and planning on the morning of the 15th. I just have a few comments in that regard. First of all, I note that the Rule 98 bis, as it's called now, the motion for acquittal, I think it was called back then, filed on behalf of Dario Kordic on March 17th, 2000, never claimed that it was solely a 7(3) case. In fact, there was 130 pages of submissions on the elements of liability under 7(1). The Defence identifies the elements of joint criminal enterprise and common purpose, because at this point in time the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision had been rendered. And the motion spends 90 pages setting out the Defence position on the facts related to these forms of liability under 7(1). It doesn't appear that the Defence perceived it as a 7(3) case at the time. The Trial Chamber's decision on the motion for acquittal, it's correct what my learned colleagues have -- the reference to the Trial Chamber decision on April 6th regarding the half-time decision, the decision on the motion to acquit, it is true that the Trial Chamber held that the evidence was sufficient to show that he was part of the high-level Herceg-Bosna community, but the Trial Chamber also stated that there was evidence of his direct involvement in nine municipalities. And the Trial Chamber stated to the Defence that they were not expected, not required and not expected to call evidence on the other 22 municipalities, that they would have to deal with the nine. Now, those nine municipalities and the evidence which was presented at the halfway time demonstrate quite clearly that Mr. Kordic was directly involved. It's not a 7(3) case or a vicarious liability case. It's a 7(1) case based on common criminal plan. He indicates that this was essentially the sole meeting which ties Dario Kordic into the direct activity on the ground. Well, in fact, the Trial Chamber found many other instances where there was direct involvement. On the night of April 16, 1993, Dario Kordic's meeting with Kraljevic, the commander of Vitezovi, just outside Vitez at the Vitezovi headquarters, and the Trial Chamber finds that they're looking over a piece of paper with a map drawn on it, discussing what needs to be done. There's a finding that he was leading military operations in Novi Travnik in 1992. There's a finding that he was leading military operations in Novi Travnik in 1992. There's a finding regarding his role in relation to the transport of weapons and operations. That's at paragraph 553. There's a finding of a report on November 1992 about the arrest of the HVO military police in Kruscica and the presence of Kordic at the Travnik HVO headquarters, where the decision was made to launch an operation to release the patrol. It's clear that this was not a 7(3) case or a vicarious liability. It was a case of his direct involvement as a planner, as an orderer, as an instigator, but actually as someone who is the prime mover in a common criminal plan in Central Bosnia. Now, my learned friend may respond that: Well, that's his definition of vicarious liability. He's not the one on the ground that's getting his hands dirty. He's not the one that's committing the crimes. Well, the planning of the meeting on April the 15th is not Dario Kordic on the ground committing the crimes. The planning on April 15th, which is not a new case by the Prosecution but just one more piece of evidence of his role in planning, instigating, or ordering. If I can now turn to the submissions in relation to Witness AT. As I've indicated, contrary to my learned colleague's very forceful submissions, this case does not come down to a two-hour meeting one afternoon in April. This microscopic approach actually doesn't do justice to a Trial Chamber's judgement which attempts to encompass acts from May of 1992. I've listed in my previous submissions examples of the direct involvement of Mr. Kordic: Travnik, releasing prisoners. There's the finding, of course, that he's involved in the joint military meetings, the joint military working group. I note that these are working group meetings for military. This is not a political meeting. And he's even perceived by the officers there to be Blaskic's superior. There's ample evidence from Busovaca, from Central Bosnia, from Kiseljak, of his direct involvement over an extensive period of time. This case is not about one meeting. In fact, the Court could have been -- could have easily convicted Mr. Kordic without AT's evidence. There's often cases where members at the high-ranking -- where you don't have, because of the fact that insiders don't come forward or because you don't have the evidence linking, directly linking a high-ranking official, where the only inference to be drawn on circumstantial evidence is that they were involved in a mode of participation which results in their criminal liability. In fact, AT's evidence actually corroborates the rest of the case, as opposed to the other way around. A few submissions I wish to make regarding the concept of corroboration. First of all, I would note that, first of all, there's no need for corroboration in the Tribunal. I think that's fairly evident. Hearsay is admissible, and you can convict in this Tribunal on hearsay evidence, even uncorroborated hearsay evidence. I point out the decision in Kunarac where the Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Kovac of the rape of Witness AB. Witness AB was a young woman who, after being raped, was sold to some soldiers, and she was never seen again. This is certainly a very tragic incident, but the legal principle still stands, and it doesn't differ just because of the nature of the evidence. The Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Kovac as a result of another witness explaining what AB confided in her. That witness, FWS-75, gave evidence that AB confided in her as to the rape. AB did not testify. There was lots of evidence which showed that Witness FWS-75 was a believable witness. There was evidence which corroborated her as a credible witness, but there isn't any other evidence that I could find of the rape, of the actual acts or the acts for which at the time the rape was -- took place. In the Appeals Chamber judgement, at paragraphs 267 and 268, the Appeals Chamber reaffirms it's settled jurisprudence that corroboration is not legally required and that corroborative testimony only goes to weight. It then refers to the fact that the appellant focused on two incidents in his appeal, one being Witness 75 and Witness AB, and it refers to previous testimony where it's recalled that AB confided in Witness 75 that the appellant had raped her. The Appeals Chamber upheld that conviction for the rape of Witness AB even though it was hearsay evidence originating from another witness. There's a difference of opinion between the Prosecution in the submissions in the brief regarding what constitutes corroboration and the submissions of the appellant. Essentially, the appellant has begun by saying that corroboration has to be corroboration in the sense of a material particular, a material fact, and has narrowed his focus as his submission proceeded to the point where there's absolutely no corroboration of the meeting on the 15th of April. With respect, there's no need for corroboration of the meeting in the sense of evidence showing the meeting on the 15th of April. If that was the case, we'd have duplicate evidence directly implicating him, we wouldn't have corroborative evidence of the witness who says that there was a meeting on the 15th of April. Corroborative evidence is not limited to evidence which mirrors AT's evidence. Corroborative evidence is evidence which tends to convince the trier of fact that a witness is telling the truth. There are different types of evidence that can be corroborative, but it's not limited to proof that the accused committed the crime. The appellant refers to an interlocutory appeal, the Appeals Chamber decision in Kordic on an interlocutory appeal on the 18th of September 2000, and he was kind enough to point it out to me at the break, for the proposition that corroboration has to be to a material particular or a material fact. Now, even if there has to be corroboration to a material fact, and that's not the Prosecution's submission, the Defence position that it has to show, go right to the meeting on the 15th of April does not necessarily follow. There can be many other material particulars in the testimony that can be corroborated which would tend to cause this Court, as did the Trial Chamber, to believe the testimony of the witness. In my respectful submission, you don't have to limit it to a material fact. The triers of fact have to decide on the basis of the evidence that is corroborative whether it convinces you that the person is telling the truth. The nature of that evidence is for the trier of fact to decide. The interlocutory appeal in Kordic dealt with Rule 94 ter at the time, and the focus in that case was the admission of affidavit evidence to support a fact in dispute. The subject matter was whether the evidence supports a fact in dispute because that was the requirement of the Rule. Rule 94 says you must bring evidence which supports a fact in dispute. So the focus was on what was a fact in dispute. It's not a decision as to what constitutes corroborative evidence, and though it does refer to the fact that there -- any evidence to support a 94 ter affidavit must be focused on the facts that it's supposed to support, that's a direct reading of Rule 94 ter. In my respectful submission, there was no dealing by the Appeals Chamber and no submissions on the scope of corroboration and whether corroboration requires corroboration of a material particular or whether it can be any evidence which tends to convince the trier of fact that the witness is telling the truth. Without going through all the evidence, it's quite clear, in my respectful submission, that, first of all, there is ample evidence that shows AT is telling the truth. Secondly, there's ample evidence which is corroborative of Witness AT which connects Kordic to the crimes. There's the nature of the campaign itself. There's the war diary. There's the meetings that I've listed, for example, in Vitezovi -- with the Vitezovi, and there's the orders for the attack. As I'm coming to the end of my submissions and to leave time for my colleagues tomorrow, I just want to mention a few concluding comments. The lying alibi defence referred to by my learned friend arose from a circumstance where the Trial Chamber corrected counsel for Kordic which said that AT himself had asked the Court to overlook his lies. The Court says wait a minute, AT didn't ask the Court to overlook his lies, and he corrects him and says it's more appropriately and more properly characterised as his defence. With respect, I don't see that correction by the Trial Chamber as somehow changing its understanding that AT gave a false alibi to the Trial Chamber. There is reference to witnesses Grubesic and Maric and others as men of substance. I'd ask you to take a look at the Prosecution's response, for example, to Mr. Grubesic at paragraphs 3.180 through to 3.185, where it lists on three separate occasions that the Trial Chamber found Mr. Grubesic not capable of belief. For Mr. Maric, his evidence is even more incredible, and if you look at paragraph 3.194 of the Prosecution's response, Mr. Maric, who is the president of Busovaca at the time of the attack, says that when his town was under attack and when plans are being made to carry out operations in the area, he went home at 3.00 p.m. in the afternoon. He was unaware of the significant press conference by Kordic and Blaskic, his political and military superior, and he never came back from his home to see what the military and civilian response was in the very town that he's the mayor. No one came to see him and no one communicated with him, and he knew nothing about the meeting and knew nothing about it and was at home for the day. Extremely -- it's highly unbelievable. Lastly, in relation to Witness AT, the trial Court was fully aware of the particular nature of his evidence and the difficulties involved in the assessment of its reliability. The Defence was given ample opportunity, and the submissions that they've made to you today were all made to the Trial Chamber and were put in cross-examination to Witness AT. The Court did not rely on AT exclusively and found that there was corroborative evidence. They examined the witness's reasons for testifying. They verified his accuracy, the consistency, and the voluntary nature of his testimony. They looked at his motivation for coming to testify before the Tribunal, and I recall the fact that he was the one that contacted the Prosecution. There was no deal made. There was no immunity given. There was, in fact, no agreement with respect to AT at the time he testified, and he subsequently made submissions before the Appeals Chamber to have his sentence reduced. He spoke of the dangers that would come to him by testifying, but he did it anyway. He didn't know what the evidence in the case was when he came and testified. He hasn't been shown to have any particular disagreement or complaint or axe to grind in respect to the people he named, Maric and Grubesic. His evidence doesn't fit with everything that the Prosecution put forward. In my respectful submission, it's not something that was catered. In fact, you may not be fully aware that the Prosecution was proceeding against Mr. Cerkez with respect to the death of an individual named Trako, and AT explained to the Prosecution that Mr. Cerkez was not liable for that, that it was another individual, and he actually exculpated Mr. Cerkez, and that was accepted. At the end of the day, the Trial Chamber heard Witness AT in full. There was extensive cross-examination. Obviously, as an Appellate Chamber, you'll be hesitant to intervene on matters related to credibility, and in this case, this was a matter that was clearly heard and adjudicated upon by the Trial Chamber. It's especially evidence that shouldn't be interfered with, where there is significant corroboration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farrell. The Appeals Chamber stays -- the hearing stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00 sharp, in this courtroom.
